title: How Harley Reid copes with the hype of being WA's most famous sportsman
text:
Harley Reid was living in the spotlight even before he was an AFL player.

In his draft year, the then-17-year old was the centre of intense debate about where he would end up playing, and since his debut with West Coast in 2024 the now 21-year old is still the centre of attention everywhere he goes.

"I think that's probably still something I'm trying to work on. It is hard, don't get me wrong," Reid told 102.5 ABC Perth's SportsTalk program.

"I've been lucky enough to get out of Perth a few times, go camping or whatnot, to reset.

"It is probably something I'm still trying to get my head around and understand."

Reid has produced a stunning season, averaging more than 24 disposals per game. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Such was the hype around his arrival in Western Australia, the state's daily paper featured him 25 times on its back page — before he had played a game.

No player before or since has been more hyped prior to their debut.

"You do definitely notice it but I just try not to let it affect me too much," Reid said after being awarded the Geoff Christian Medal as the ABC's best WA-based player.

Harley Reid was awarded the Geoff Christian medal for the 2026 season. (ABC News)

"I feel like you do get that pressure, but I feel like if my mental state's there and I've prepared well, the pressure isn't there.

"I know I've done the work. It's all about that preparation as well."

Paying the 'WA Tax'

Reid was crowned West Coast club champion on Friday night when he claimed the John Worsfold Medal and is coming off his best season, but Eagles fans will have to wait until round three in 2027 to see the midfielder in action.

West Coast unsuccessfully challenged his two-game suspension for a dangerous tackle on Hawthorn's Jai Newcombe.

"It's that WA tax. If I was playing in Victoria I reckon we'd have had a different outcome," Reid quipped.

"I was pretty disappointed with the outcome."

Reid plays the game on the edge, but is trying to rein in some of his off-the-ball antics. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

It was the latest controversy for Reid, who has given away more free kicks than any other player by this stage of their career.

He also holds the Eagles' record for free kicks conceded in a season.

"I think playing with aggression and bringing that competitive edge is a big part of my game," Reid said.

"I feel at times, me playing on the edge compared to other players, I feel like I've been targeted a lot more in different areas.

"It's just about making sure I'm using my aggression in the right areas and winning the contest, tackling hard and competing for the footy without letting it take me away from my job."

Doing the extra work

Reid is one of the Eagles young stars that the club hopes, along with the likes of Willem Duursma and Reuben Ginbey, will lead them back to the top of the AFL mountain.

The Eagles hope Willem Duursma and Reid are the young stars that will lead them back to the AFL Finals. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire)

And they are doing everything they can to do just that, including establishing the Matt Priddis Academy, named in honour of the 2014 Brownlow medallist, which sees the first-to-fourth year players do a session together each week.

"That's created a great camaraderie between the group and I think it's going to hold us in good stead for the years to come," Reid said.

"For us, it's extra education, extra skills for our mental and physical [sharpness] and just more of the game plan so we keep filtering it through.

"Sometimes it's harder to learn in a massive group so it's just more bringing that group closer together and making sure that education and knowledge that gets passed through is getting soaked into us."

title: Tassie cheers on 'fantastic' Devils in first ever home finals clash
text:
Crowds of passionate Devils fans have braved the wet weather to show up for Tassie's VFL semi-final clash against the bombers in North Hobart.

Tasmania Devils daring to dream The Devils weren't supposed to make the VFL finals. They were barely even supposed to be in the league.

A team that is in their inaugural season, a win today would secure Tasmania a place in a VFL preliminary final.

To get over the line, the Devils will have to overcome Essendon, who are on a seven-game winning streak, and a potential downpour.

At the end of half time, Essendon was leading the match by 8 points, with 57 points to the Devils' 49.

As gates opened at North Hobart on Saturday, the enthusiasm from fans decked out in green, donning raincoats and racing to get undercover seats, wasn't to be dampened.

Lee and Lucy Edwards have full confidence the Devils have what it takes to get a win over the Bombers. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

For Lucy and Lee Edwards, there was no where else they'd rather be.

"I don't care — rain, hail or shine, let's go," Ms Edwards said.

"We played really well earlier in the year in York park when it rained cats and dogs, and we got over the line there. So I'm down — let's rain again and we'll win again with any luck."

Thomas Brown has seen nearly all the Devils VFL games in their inaugural season. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Mr Edwards said, no matter the result, for the club to make it this far in their first season was an achievement in itself.

" For a new team, this is fantastic. Tassie go on, come on! "

Decked out in her beanie and wet weather gear, Devils fan Ann Sigley was hoping she had a secret weapon with her in the stands — a bear in hand-knitted kit, named "mini Rum'un".

She said it took her four days to make the mini mascot, which is just one in her AFL collection.

Ann Sigley spent several months making a little Rum'un to show support for the Devils. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

"He shouts loud," she said, with a smile. "Goes up in the air a few times.

"I tell you what, if we get into the finals, I'm going there too. Over to Melbourne."

Among the sea of green, there were a few flickers of red and black. One of the brave Bombers supporters was Wynyard man Manassa Walker.

He said he was feeling confident going into the match, with the Essendon side including 18 AFL listed players, including former Devil, Jackson Artemis.

Manassa Walker from Wynyard is not scared to be surrounded by a sea of green and hopes the Bombers come away with a win. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

Mr Walker said, with a few Wynyard boys in the Tassie side he would also be barracking for them, but ultimately he was a "bomber at heart".

It was a similar sentiment shared by James Rogerson, who, wearing a Devils jumper and a Bombers scarf, was in for a win either way.

"I think football wins for the day," he said.

The dreary weather wasn't enough to stop droves of passionate supporters attending the clash. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

He said the Devils making it into a semi final, played at home, was a feat in itself.

"It's well above expectations, I think.

"They're doing really well. They've really gelled together as a team after only one pre-season together. I think they're doing really well."

Sophie Davis is among the thousands of Tasmanians supporting the Devils at North Hobart Oval today. (ABC News: Kate Nickels)

For the young Davis family, watching their team was the perfect way to start the morning.

Daughter Sophie said she never doubted that the Devils would make it to to the semi finals.

"Of course. They're the Devils!"

title: Ben Simmons signs multi-million-dollar NBA deal with Kings
text:
Australian former number one overall draft pick Ben Simmons has taken a significant step towards resurrecting his NBA career, agreeing to a one-year deal with the Sacramento Kings.

The Melbourne-born guard returns on a $US3.5 million ($4.9 million) contract after sitting ‌out the entire 2025-26 campaign while rehabilitating back and leg injuries that have hampered him in recent years.

Simmons, who last played with the Los Angeles Clippers in April 2025, celebrated his Kings deal on social media on Saturday morning (AEST) by posting a photograph of himself wearing a team cap.

While reigniting Simmons's NBA career, his latest move is also a step towards possible Australian Boomers selection for next year's FIBA World Cup in Qatar and the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.

The Boomers, under Washington Wizards assistant and former NBL guard Adam Caporn, are chasing a podium return after a breakthrough bronze medal at the Tokyo Olympics five years ago.

Simmons spent his year out of basketball rebuilding his body and gathered momentum in his comeback bid during a Boomers mini-camp in Melbourne last month.

The former Philadelphia 76ers (2017-21), Brooklyn Nets (2022-25) and Clippers (2024-25) guard also reportedly attracted serious attention from the reigning champion New York Knicks and Golden State Warriors before he signed with Sacramento.

Simmons was drafted as the No.1 overall by Philadelphia in 2016, but missed his entire first season with a foot injury before establishing himself as one of the league's brightest young stars.

He claimed 2017-18 rookie ‌of the year honours and was a two-time All-Defensive ​pick before further injuries derailed his career.

Simmons has not played more than 58 games ​in ​a season since 2018-19.

He ​has averaged 13.1 points, ‌7.4 rebounds, 7.2 assists and 1.5 steals in 383 career games (344 starts) with the 76ers, Nets and Clippers.

Sacramento open the NBA preseason at home against the Los Angeles Lakers on October ​5, and visit the Clippers for their regular-season opener on ​October 21.

The Kings were 22-60 last season, finishing 14th in the Western Conference, and have only reached the playoffs once since 2006.

They suffered a first-round loss to Golden State in 2023, and have not won a playoff series since 2004.

AAP

title: Williams sisters knocked out by Aussie Joint and Chan
text:
Australian Maya Joint has again spoiled the part for the legendary Williams sisters, teaming up with Hao-Ching Chan to knock Serena and Venus out of the first round of the US Open women's doubles.

In front of a packed and passionate crowd at Arthur Ashe Stadium, Joint and Chan came from 0-5 down in the deciding 10-point tiebreaker to down the legendary sisters 6-3, 6-7 (6/8), 7-6 (10/7).

This is the second consecutive grand slam that Joint has played spoiler, knocking Serena out in the first round of the Wimbledon ladies singles on Centre Court.

After losing the second set in a tiebreaker, Joint and Chan were in control of the third set with a 4-1 lead, before the Williams sisters fought back.

Serena Williams (right) of the United States and Venus Williams (left) of the United States in action against Hao-Ching Chan of Chinese Taipei and Maya Joint of Australia in the first round of doubles on Day 6 of the US Open at USTA Billie Jean King National Tennis Center on September 04, 2026 in New York City (Getty Images: Robert Prange)

Serena and Venus looked set for a dream comeback win when they held a huge 5-0 lead in the first to 10.

But both sisters double-faulted as Joint and Chan won 10 of the final 12 points to take the match.

The Williams sisters were supposed to make their grand slam doubles return at Wimbledon, but had to pull out after Serena hurt her knee.

That delayed their return to the Grand Slam stage until New York, where they won in 1999 and 2009 and are now 27-8 in their 10 appearances.

The match got a spot in the night session in Arthur Ashe Stadium — practically unheard of for first-round doubles.

The sisters were once dominant in women's doubles, teaming to win 14 grand slam titles along with Olympic gold medals in 2000, 2008 and 2012. They shared the number one ranking in women's doubles for eight weeks.

It appeared a first-round loss in 2022 was their last time together, with Serena stepping away from tennis that year after winning 23 Grand Slam singles titles. She came back this summer and now has two heartbreaking defeats with her older sister. They also lost in a match tiebreaker at the Cincinnati Open.

Venus Williams also lost in the first round of singles.

ABC/AP

title: That viral 'bulls***' moment and how football saved Awer Mabil
text:
Awer Mabil will never forget his first football, because he made it himself.

"We used to collect plastic bags and then tie them up into a ball shape," he tells triple j hack.

"It was pretty cool."

Loading...

Mabil is remembering his childhood in the Kakuma Refugee Camp where he was born in north-western Kenya.

"Football was 100 per cent an escape for us," he says.

"If you're hungry, you don't feel hungry because you're just playing for the moment with your friends.

"Then when I came to Australia, I was like, 'oh … I don't have to make the balls from the scratch.'"

Mabil and his family arrived in Australia as refugees when he was 10-years-old.

Since then he's established himself as one of Australia's most well-known football players, representing the nation at two World Cups, and being recognised as the Young Australian of the Year in 2023.

Awer Mabil has become one of Australia's most recognisable footballers and was named Young Australian of the Year in 2023. (AAP Image/Dave Hunt) (AAP: Dave Hunt)

Now 30, Mabil is back in Australia after a decade playing in Europe, achieving his dreams.

Earlier this year, the Socceroos star signed a three-year deal with Melbourne City and says he's looking forward to putting some roots down here.

"I can finally buy furniture that I can keep," he laughs.

" I also want to play in front of my family and friends ... I didn't take advantage of it when I was here before and now I get that chance again. "

'We're all proud'

Returning to Adelaide from the Socceroos World Cup campaign in July, Mabil made headlines when he was asked about One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's calls for a "monoculture" in Australia.

Loading TikTok content

"It's just all bulls***," Mabil told waiting reporters.

Now with a few months distance, the football player says he's still surprised by how much traction his response got.

"To be honest, it just came to my head," he tells hack.

"I was just being myself.

"I feel passionate about including everybody because that's what makes Australia great.

"So if there are people that try to divide what Australia is then that's not good."

Mabil says it's important to not only tolerate other cultures in Australia, but celebrate them.

"My little brothers were born here and they're more Aussie than anybody else.

"But everybody's got different flavours."

Mabil says many have thrown their support behind his defence of multiculturalism in recent months, but concedes there has been hate as well.

"I don't let that energy get to me."

"I've learned that being genuine, being pure to yourself and honest is best.

"Don't take in negativity."

Returning to Kakuma

One of Awer Mabil's biggest focuses in life, away from sport, is charity.

After a trip back to the camp where he was born, he and his brother started the charity Barefoot to Boots which supports refugees living in camps around the world by supplying them with football boots and equipment.

"It's very humbling," he says.

"Every time I go back it brings me back to appreciating the life that I have, that we have here in Australia, because people are struggling with the basic stuff there."

Non-government organisation Barefoot to Boots uses soccer to tackle global inequality and promote "health, education and gender equality initiatives" in refugee camps, especially at Kakuma in Kenya. Photo taken in 2018. (Facebook: Barefoot to Boots)

Barefoot to Boots has expanded its scope in recent years, funding sanitary products for girls, hospital equipment, teaching supplies and building public bathrooms.

"We went into the hospitals and realised the premature born kids didn't have a chance.

"So we donated three incubators and to be honest that's the best thing we've ever done because that's saving lives."

'Learn to love yourself'

Mabil says a bit of time has helped him better appreciate the Socceroos' effort at this year's World Cup, after the Australian team was beaten in a Round of 32 clash against Egypt.

It was just the third time the Socceroos had reached the knockout stage of the tournament.

"We were so close to making history," he says.

"We should be proud as a team.

"The future is looking great and I'm very optimistic about Australian football."

Socceroos star Awer Mabil isn't sure what will come after his football but says he will tackle whatever comes next with the same dedication as his playing career. (triple j hack: Arianna Lucente)

Asked what his future holds after football, Mabil smiles.

"It's an interesting question.

"I enjoy media a lot and could go down that path.

" But whatever I choose next … I'll put the same discipline into it that I did towards my football career. "

His advice for other young Australians who may be struggling with identity or feeling different is simple.

"Learn to love yourself.

"Remember … I'm created perfectly the way I am."

title: Clarkson opens up about 'publicly humilating' Kangaroos axing
text:
Alastair Clarkson says he and his family have been "publicly humiliated" by the way North Melbourne handled his sacking as head coach.

Clarkson has given his first interview since being let go by the Kangaroos on Wednesday.

Kangaroos president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney were brutally honest at their media conference in explaining why Clarkson was sacked with a year to go on his contract.

Clarkson, a four-time premiership coach at Hawthorn, said his family felt insulted by Hood and Viney's appearance in front of reporters.

"We're just shocked, and we just thought we were owed a little bit of respect in being informed and warned," Clarkson told The Age.

Alastair Clarkson leaves North North Melbourne president Sonja Hood and football boss Todd Viney explain why the club is parting ways with Alastair Clarkson with a year to run on his deal.

"Instead, they chose to dance on my grave like this."

Clarkson, who coached the Kangaroos for four seasons, added: "We all feel … so publicly humiliated."

He rejected suggestions his relationships with players and staff had deteriorated.

"Is that all my fault, is it?" Clarkson said.

"My mantra has never changed, and that has been to have care and empathy to help players chase their dream.

"I feel like my life's shot."

Premiership coaches John Longmire and Adam Simpson have been floated as options to take over from Clarkson, due to their stature as champion former Kangaroos players.

But after watching first-time coaches Steven King and Josh Fraser succeed this year, the Kangaroos could be inclined to find a highly rated assistant.

Jaymie Graham (Fremantle), Corey Enright (St Kilda) and James Kelly (Geelong) were in contention for the Carlton job, before Fraser's results as interim coach made him the only choice for the Blues.

AAP

title: Fewer kids open books for fun, prompting calls for national reading strategy
text:
From a last-minute Where's Wally to a classic Harry Potter, kids across Australia dressed up as their favourite literary characters to celebrate Book Week in August.

But literacy and library organisations across Australia are concerned that kids are more interested in their costumes for Book Week, than actually reading the books that inspired them.

A new declaration released to coincide with Book Week says more needs to be done to encourage reading, improve literacy, and boost library funding across Australian schools.

The Statement on School Libraries and Reading for Pleasure was produced by the Australian Library and Information Association, the Australian Coalition for School Libraries, and literacy not-for-profit Australia Reads.

The declaration calls on the federal government to make school libraries mandatory, and ensure they are properly resourced and staffed.

Australia Reads chief executive Anna Burkey said the statement was part of her organisation's call for a national reading strategy.

Anna Burkey is calling for a national reading strategy. (Supplied: Anna Burkey)

"Things like Book Week happen because of volunteer organisations like the Children's Book Council and the hearts and souls of parents, teachers and librarians making it happen," Ms Burkey said.

"But we want more support and investment in reading as an infrastructure.

"We need a national plan."

She said it was often children in lower economic regions that did not have sufficient access to books.

"It becomes a postcode lottery," she said.

" I was at a private school yesterday and it had five librarians but you go five miles down the road and there's a school that has no library or librarians. "

What the stats say

A 2025 study from the University of South Australia found that children and teenagers were reading less than in previous years, if at all.

The study into post-pandemic after-school activities found that fewer young people were reading for pleasure.

Sarah Mayor Cox says people should prioritise the joy of reading. (Supplied: Mark Leonardi)

In 2019, 10.8 per cent of children never read for fun; in 2022, the figure had climbed to 52.5 per cent.

By comparison, daily social media use had increased from 26 per cent in 2019 to 85.4 per cent in 2022.

The study's results are reflected in the nation's NAPLAN results from recent years.

During 2023, NAPLAN reading results showed that 74.5 per cent of year 5 students were reading at a strong or exceeding level, compared to 2026 where that figure has decreased to 71 per cent.

Ms Burkey said the drop in reading was not just in children, but adults too, with 30 per cent of all Australians not picking up a book in the last year.

"We have more choices than ever before for entertainment," she said.

Ms Burkey said there were plenty of positives as well.

"Even if a third of people in Australia is not reading, that still means the vast majority are," she said.

" The other good news story is that half of Australians want to read more often. "

How to get kids reading

Literary consultant and Bendigo-based author Sarah Mayor Cox said literacy skills often fell off the list for struggling families, which is why programs such as the late Dolly Parton's Imagination Library were so important.

"A child can have their own mini library by the time they age out of the program," Ms Mayor Cox said of the Imagination Library.

"It gives them such a head start before they start school or kindergarten."

According to the Grattan Institute, one in three children can not read proficiently at their grade level.

Sarah Mayor Cox says literacy skills often fall off the list for struggling families. (Supplied: Sarah Mayor Cox)

Ms Mayor Cox said prioritising the joy of reading over the technical skills was foundational for getting children to read for fun, and eventually their literacy skills would improve.

"There is this obsession with technical reading, such as phonics," she said.

" People should prioritise the joy of reading over competency. "

Ms Burkey agreed, saying the relationship between literacy skills and reading for leisure was critical and the benefits were "life-changing".

She said often people could feel overwhelmed with the choices of books, and it could be an obstacle for those wanting to read more.

But she said the best way to encourage kids to read more was to support their choices.

"Supporting them to test and trial, finding out what they like is really important [as is] validating what they choose," Ms Burkey said.

"It doesn't really matter what they choose.

"If they are excited by that, amazing, lean in."

title: Aussie star Myers beats Olympic champions to win Diamond League Final
text:
Australia's Cameron Myers has recorded the most significant win of his young career by taking out the men's 1,500 metres at the Diamond League Final in Brussels.

Myers became only the eighth Australian to win a Diamond League Final title when he clocked a time of three minutes and 30.14 seconds at the King Baudouin Stadium.

The 20-year-old beat home a stacked field featuring the two most recent Olympic champions in the event, the USA's Cole Hocker and Norwegian Jakob Ingebrigtsen.

"I wouldn't say this victory comes as a surprise to me," Myers said after the race.

"It's more a relief to finally showcase what I've been building toward over the last couple of years.

"It feels surreal, even though I always believed I had it in me. But it's so different to actually do it and actually execute it when it matters.

"This is going to be a fun memory to look back on."

Cameron Myers (right) pipped Kenya's Phanuel Koech to claim victory. (Getty Images: Tim Clayton)

Myers timed his final sprint in the home straight to perfection, narrowly edging out Kenyan teenager Phanuel Koech (3:30.18) and American Ethan Strand (3:30.50).

Ingebrigtsen, who was the Tokyo Olympic gold medallist, posted a time of 3:30.52 to finish in fourth place, with Hocker seventh in 3:30.80.

Coached by Dick Telford, Myers is the best Australian prospect in the men's 1,500m since 1960 Olympic champion Herb Elliott.

The Brussels victory is the latest chapter in the Canberran's stellar season.

Myers set a national record of 3:28.00 in winning the 1,500m at the Paris Diamond League meet in June.

The time is the second-fastest run in the world this year.

Myers won the mile (3:46.06) at another Diamond League meet, Eugene's Prefontaine Classic, in July and finished second to Scottish world-record holder Josh Kerr in the same event at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

Less than a week ago, Myers triumphed in the 1,500m (3:30.96) at Berlin's prestigious ISTAF meet.

Kurtis Marschall finished third in the men's pole vault. (Getty Images: Richard Heathcote)

Among other Australian results in Brussels, Kurtis Marschall was third on countback in the men's pole vault.

Marschall and second-placed Sondre Guttormsen of Norway both cleared 5.82m, with Greece's Emmanouil Karalis winning with a meet record of 6.12m.

Sweden's Olympic and world champion, Mondo Duplantis, was a late withdrawal due to leg tightness.

Lachlan Kennedy ran under 10 seconds for the fifth time this season in the men's 100m, posting 9.99 to be fourth behind winner and reigning world champion, Jamaica's Oblique Seville (9.90).

Matthew Denny was also fourth in the men's discus with a best throw of 68.04m.

Slovenian Kristjan Čeh produced a meet record of 71.29m to claim victory.

Two-time Commonwealth Games champion Rose Davies also just missed the podium in the women's 5,000m, finishing fourth in 14:37.47 behind Ethiopian victor Freweyni Hailu (14:35.20).

Fellow Australians Georgia Griffith (14:38.69) and Linden Hall (14:40.62) were sixth and 10th respectively.

title: Broome disappears into thick fog as WA wet season nears
text:
A thick blanket of fog engulfed Broome, in Western Australia's far north, this week with visibility limited to less than 50 metres.

The weather bureau said it was a sign the tropical dry season had come to an end, and the hot semi-arid Broome climate was on the precipice of entering the wet season.

Residents heading about their morning activities on Wednesday described the "eerie" magical feeling of being surrounded by dense fog.

Fog is a common occurrence during September in Broome. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Cable Beach blanketed

Broome resident Hilary Wilkins described a strange scene on Wednesday morning.

"When I woke up, it was suspiciously quiet out there; normally you can hear aircraft taking off where I live," she said.

"So I got in the car to go to the beach with the dog and it was absolutely thick fog, dripping off the roof."

Once Ms Wilkins was on the beach, she saw yacht masts "sticking out of the fog" as the sun was rising, catching glints of light.

"As I walked down the beach there was this really cool, what I call a fog bow, it's literally like a rainbow, but with the blue sky coming through the fog," she said.

"I thought, 'This will be a cracking shot if I can get the dog in the middle of the bow.'"

Jane Meade was also walking her dogs on the beach and said her visibility was as little as 30 metres.

Jane Meade driving through the fog in Broome. (Supplied: Jane Meade)

"It's really eerie because with the fog being so thick, you can stand on the beach and not actually see anything," she said.

"It reminds me of my travels overseas being in the USA and waking up in the morning listening to the foghorns in Santa Barbara."

What causes fog?

BOM senior forecaster Jonathan How said fog formed due to the amount of moisture in the air and when night temperatures fell.

At the weather bureau, fog is measured if visibility falls below 300 metres, with anything above that considered mist.

The visibility on Wednesday got below 50 metres at Broome Airport and persisted for nine hours, soaking Broome up to the Dampier Peninsula.

Jonathan How says the foggy mornings indicate the dry season is coming to an end. (Supplied: BOM)

Mr How said it was typical this time of year, as Broome headed towards the wetter months.

"So certainly people might be noticing a bit more fog on the forecast over the next few days and weeks," he said.

" Hopefully everyone enjoyed the dry season because the humidity is really starting to pick up. "

Mr How said safety concerns on the road should be considered and advised people to drive to conditions and take precautions.

He said seeing how fog affected different parts of WA's vast state was interesting, reaffirming it was indeed the "Kimberley's turn" for this weather occurrence.

"Western Australia spans tropical climates in the north and then cool Mediterranean South," he said.

"So not surprisingly, we do see quite a variation in climate across the state, not just month-to-month, but also day-to-day."

Yawuru seasons

Broome's traditional owners, the Yawuru people, have six different seasons relating to the changes in climate.

These are Man-gala, Marrul, Wirralburu, Barrgana, Wirlburu and Laja.

The current season is Wirlburu, aligning with the re-emergence of foggy morning as the weather slowly starts to warm up.

Coco Yu is a Yawuru language specialist, teacher, mentor, and translator, working at the Mabu Yawuru Ngan-ga Language Centre. (Supplied)

Coco Yu from the Yawuru Language Centre said Wirlburu was a short transition season.

"The two big seasons for us are wet season, which is Man-gala, and the cold season was just Barrgana, and then we have these little ones in between usually connected to wind," she said.

"Wirlburu could last for one or two weeks, it's just one of those little things when sea breeze starts to blow and the day starts to warm up a bit."

Ms Yu said she felt awareness around Yawuru seasons was growing in the community.

Wirlburu was everyone's favourite season, according to Ms Yu, because the combination of sun and breezes were a relief before it got too hot.

title: Country pub owner proud to keep 'heartbeat' of town going at 86
text:
Jim Pohl has lost count of how many pubs he has owned, although the 86-year-old publican's memory is sharp as a tack.

"I got the feeling it might have been 15 or 16, maybe 17," he said.

Jim was 26 when he immigrated from Malaysia. He joined the air force and even worked in abattoirs before venturing into the publican scene.

Jim Pohl had many roles before settling into his publican career. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

He was working at a Katherine pub in the Northern Territory when a chance comment from his boss sparked the change.

"An old lady says to me, 'You're wasting your time working for me, you should go and get your own pub,'" Jim said.

Country 'heartbeat'

He soon bought a pub south of Perth in North Dandalup.

"From there, one thing led to another," Jim said.

He has since owned 16 pubs, mostly in regional WA, spanning from Northampton in the Midwest to Mount Barker in the Great Southern.

Jim ran two pubs in Perth, but "didn't cotton on to the city life".

"I just kept going to the bush. Better people, greater atmosphere and people are real in the bush," he said.

The pub draws in the local characters. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

"You're dealing with real people, real everyday people, people who get their hands dirty and know what it's all about, you know, what work is.

" The pub is the heartbeat of a country town. "

A family affair

Now, Jim has settled in Perenjori, 350 kilometres north-east of Perth, working at the hotel with his son, Kirk.

The kitchen can churn out up to 100 meals a night, drawing in a bumper crowd every "T-bone Tuesday".

Kirk Pohl is busy in the kitchen each T-bone Tuesday. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Each day, Jim is up before the sun to prepare the evening special.

"I do it all in the morning, prepare it for [Kirk], it's ready for him at four o'clock, and I go and give him a hand if he needs it," Jim said.

" Then I sit at the end of the bar and just make sure that the barmaids are working. "

Kirk and Jim Pohl agree that good staff can make or break the pub. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Mr Matchmaker

Kirk has followed in his father's footsteps, owning and managing the Perenjori Hotel since 2005.

"I grew up in pubs," Kirk said,

With that kind of upbringing, Kirk learnt the keys to success.

"Just the basic things like cold beer and a warm shower and a good bed," he said.

"Staff make a big difference … they can really make or break."

The pub hosts a cycle of international backpackers working behind the bar — but some never leave.

Silvia Pohl met her husband, Kirk, while working at the pub. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Over the years, 13 women have fallen in love with Perenjori locals and put roots down in Australia, including Kirk's wife, Silvia.

"She actually got off the bus here as a backpacker on her 27th birthday," he said.

"She was travelling from Italy and she just wound up getting a job with us here and the rest is history I suppose."

Kirk and Silvia now have two children, but Jim also claims the other 21 children born to couples who met at the pub as his grandchildren.

"I won a medal from the immigration department," he jokes.

Loading...

In path of destruction

Jim was sleeping on the second floor of the hotel when Cyclone Seroja struck in 2021.

The category 3 storm damaged more than 2,270 properties across the Midwest and Wheatbelt, including the Perenjori Hotel.

"I heard a crack and I though, 'Oh bloody God'," Jim says.

"A whole chimney … flew past me.

"[It] hit the power pole in the corner there, snapped it in half and sent the whole town black."

The Pohls rebuilt after Cyclone Seroja. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Once dawn broke, Jim assessed the damage.

"The whole roof got blown across the road," he said.

Insurance offered to pay out the damage but the Pohls chose to stay and rebuild, and the hotel re-opened in 2023.

"I'd just been selling all my pubs and this was the only one that I kept for him [Kirk]," Jim says.

"So they fixed it up for us, and there you go, we're trading again.

" And [it's] probably one of the better pubs in the Midwest, here, even if I say so. "

Jim Pohl may be biased but says the pub is one of the best in the region. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

No retirement plans

Jim says he has no plans to retire.

"I need something to worry about tomorrow, I have to have a reason to get up in the morning — and smelling the roses, I'm not ready for that," he says.

" That's what it is, a reason for living. "

Jim Pohl is still hands-on in the kitchen, sometimes churning up to 100 meals a night. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

With a few minutes until the pub opens, a handful of regular customers are waiting at the door.

Even the rusted-on clientele concede that Jim is doing something right.

"He makes everybody welcome," Tom Downer says.

"I can't believe I'm actually saying that about Jim, but he does."

Steve King says there is a softer side to Jim than he lets on. (ABC Midwest & Wheatbelt: Chris Lewis)

Steve King added: "He pretends he's tough, but with the staff he's like butter."

Jim attributes his success to those larrikins — his customers.

"The reason why this place trades well, it's because of the people," he says.

" You sit here, just pretend to be nobody, and I guarantee within five minutes, somebody will be talking to you. "

title: Rugby league legend walks 300km to raise $170,000 for dementia research
text:
Since being diagnosed with early-onset Alzheimer's disease five years ago, rugby league legend Royce Simmons has seen its devastating effects firsthand.

"It's pretty tough," he said.

"You meet other people with dementia … you think these people are not too bad, this person is a bit worse and this person is terrible.

"As you go on, you think you're going to go down that track, so it keeps you on edge."

The former Penrith Panthers skipper has been on a journey to help others afflicted with dementia and raise money to find a cure.

For the past 12 days, Mr Simmons has walked more than 300 kilometres from Gilgandra to Cowra in the New South Wales Central West.

Royce Simmons was diagnosed with Alzheimer's five years ago at the age of 61. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

Royce's Big Walk has raised more than $170,000 so far this year, and continues accepting donations until the end of September.

Over the past five years, the walk has raised more than $2.2 million for dementia research and support services.

"[People] think dementia is an old person's problem … I've had it now for five years and I'm 67," Mr Simmons said.

"There are a lot of people now living in their 30s, 40s and 50s who are starting to get dementia.

"It is a massive thing that everyone needs to know about."

Going home

Mr Simmons visited his birthplace of Gooloogong on Wednesday where he was met by family, friends and local schoolchildren.

"It is fantastic, I didn't expect this many people to be here," he said.

"So many people I haven't seen for a few years have all turned up."

Royce Simmons was met by family and friends when he arrived in his hometown of Gooloogong on Wednesday. (ABC News: Hamish Cole )

His sister Maria Niven was there to welcome him home to the town they grew up in.

"It is beautiful for him to be able to come back to his hometown," she said.

"I'm glad he had the idea [to do the walk], I think it is helping him cope with this rotten disease.

"I'm so proud that he can still do these things."

League legends

Mr Simmons represented the Penrith Panthers in 238 games, winning the premiership with them in 1991, and played 10 times for New South Wales and Australia.

Over the course of the walk, he was joined by a host of former rugby league players including his former teammate Brad Fittler, James Maloney and Darren Britt.

"It is great when you get so many old players that come in and want to join you, go for the walk and talk about old times," Mr Simmons said.

Former rugby league player Darren Britt joined Royce Simmons for part of his walk raising money for Dementia Australia. (ABC News: Hamish Cole )

Mr Britt described Mr Simmons as "a remarkable bloke".

"Anyone in any need, he was always out there to help them," he said.

"The hospitality we've had along the road, people coming up and bringing us biscuits and drinks... It is amazing."

Royce Simmons won the NRL premiership in 1991 with the Penrith Panthers. (Supplied: NRL Images )

Raising awareness

The money raised by the walk goes towards funding research programs to find a cure to the disease.

According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, dementia is the leading cause of death in Australia.

Royce Simmons was welcomed to his hometown of Gooloogong by students at the local school. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

About 446,000 Australians are thought to be living with a form of dementia while approximately 1.7 million people help care for someone with the condition.

"I can't walk around thinking I'm doing a good job until someone finds an answer to that," Mr Simmons said.

"If our foundation can play some part to find [a cure] that's all I'm really looking for.

"I'm not looking for too many pats on the back."

title: Heartbreak in New York as Williams sisters turn back the clock, fall just short
text:
Advertisement

SportTennisUS Open Heartbreak in New York as Williams sisters turn back the clock, fall just short Michael Koziol September 5, 2026 — 1:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Some fans have criticised this US Open for the ambient noise emitted by attendees who won’t stop talking during play – particular on its cavernous centre court. But reporters who have been at Arthur Ashe Stadium all week agreed the crowd was much better behaved at Friday night’s blockbuster starring Venus and Serena Williams. They were there to actually watch the game. Serena and Venus Williams turned back the clock in a three-hour doubles thriller at the US Open. Getty Images And so they should be. These are legends of the sport, who turned back the clock and fell agonisingly short in a doubles thriller against Australia’s Maya Joint and Taiwan’s Hao-ching Chan. It was a match that more than lived up to the occasion; getting better over its three hours, and with plenty of quality, exciting rallies that can sometimes go missing in the stop-start, rapid-fire nature of doubles tennis.

Advertisement

On a hot Friday night, New York brought out its stars. Mr Beast, the YouTuber extraordinaire who has amassed more than 500 million subscribers, was on court for the coin toss, while those watching in the stands included Vogue editor and tennis tragic Anna Wintour, Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Andy Dalton and wrestler Mr T. While the crowd may have been respectful during points, it was uproarious between them. From the moment Serena, 44, and Venus, 46, emerged on the court, the parochial New York audience went predictably crazy. The jubilant New York crowd thought the American icons were home and hosed. Getty Images It is here at the US Open that these titans won two of their 14 grand slam doubles trophies; where Venus was a singles champion twice and where Serena picked up six of her 23 singles titles. In short, they are royalty. They last played doubles here in 2022, when they were already in their 40s, losing in the first round. The stands then, as now, were packed to the rafters with fans who thought they may not see the Williams sisters again.

Advertisement

Indeed, Serena retired straight after that US Open, and gave birth to her second daughter, Adira, nearly a year later. This week she told Good Morning America her inspiration to return to the doubles court came from her older daughter, Olympia. “You need to play with Auntie VeVe,” Olympia had urged. “She said it so clear and so calm. She’s like my mom, she doesn’t really talk a lot, but when she does talk, you listen.” Australia’s Maya Joint and Hao-ching Chan of Taiwan high five after a point. AP Photo/Adam Hunger Joint, who is just 20, was born in Michigan to an Australian father, and moved to Melbourne last year. This year, she knocked Serena out of Wimbledon in the first round of the singles draw. Like a classic car that needs a few runs around the block to warm up, the Williams sisters excelled as the match went on, having lost the first set 3-6. Serena got bolder at the net, to her advantage, while Venus improved her ground strokes from the back of the court.

Advertisement

Challenged substantially multiple times on serve in the second, they dug in and, willed on by the home crowd, produced some of the best tennis of the match at the net and from the baseline. Fans roared when, after a truly remarkable rally in the tiebreak, the sisters set up their fourth set point. When they ultimately prevailed to send the match to a decider, the crowd rose instantly to its feet. Serena Williams, 23-time grand slam singles champion and 14-time doubles champ with her sister, on Friday night. AP The third and final set was no less exciting. Down a break early, the Williams sisters clawed their way back to even keel. An expectant crowd rode every wave, gasping as Serena smashed a forehand way long at 4-4, and cheering every winner (and occasionally, a fault from Chan or Joint, which the umpire tried to quell). Related Article US Open ‘Someone is smoking weed’: Sabalenka interrupts US Open match over cannabis smell

Advertisement

People were on their feet as Venus and Serena raced to a 5-0 lead in the deciding tiebreak when victory seemed all but assured. Somehow, they faltered, stymied by costly errors at the final hurdle. The crowd was subdued in defeat, but gave them a standing ovation as they departed. In the end, not much separated the contenders. One too many errant net shots, one or two double faults, a few over-hit forehands. The legends matched their younger counterparts pound for pound, they put on a thrilling show, and the win could have easily been theirs. Speaking on court after the match, Joint praised the “surreal” atmosphere, one she had not experienced before. Playing against such esteemed opponents was “super special”, she said. “I grew up in Michigan, I’ve always looked up to them … I’m lost for words.” Fans left the stadium heartbroken but not disappointed after the Williams sisters were beaten in three sets. Getty Images We often write off older bodies, especially women who have given birth. It is something every elite athlete must grapple with; on the men’s side, Novak Djokovic is doing just that after his first-round exit from the US Open at age 39, having vomited multiple times on court as he appeared to come to grips with his new limitations.

Advertisement

Venus and Serena Williams declined to speak to reporters after the match, so there was no opportunity to parse their thoughts on the gutting loss. But they turned back the clock with style – and though many left the stadium heartbroken, nobody left disappointed. Watch the US Open live on 9GO!, 9NOW and Stan Sport. Kathmandu: Relatives with the grim task of identifying their loved ones missing in Nepal’s catastrophic floods go filing through the gates of Kathmandu’s Maharajgunj Medical Campus, uncertain of what they will see, or what they want to find. The morgue is a stopover for many of the bodies recovered from remote Rasuwa and Nuwakot, the worst hit districts. Forensic teams take DNA samples and attach tags, then send the bodies to temporary mass graves outside the capital, making way for the next batch. Loading For families whose desperate combing of the hospital have come to naught, each load of bodies at the morgue holds closure or promise.

Advertisement

“I hope he is still alive and I don’t find him here,” says 24-year-old Bakhat Pariyar, who is checking for his little brother, Laxman. “But if he is dead, we need to take him home to perform our rituals.” Laxman last made contact with his family at 7.30am on August 26, the day of the flood, near the wiped-out village of Timure. Pariyar says his brother was almost certain to be granted a study visa for the United Kingdom and had wanted to go trekking in the spectacular mountains one last time. Bakhat Pariyar at Kathmandu’s Maharajgunj Medical Campus, moments after looking through pages of photos of unidentified bodies. He is searching for his younger brother Laxman, a student who was last seen in Timure just before flash flooding hit the area. KATE GERAGHTY He is not among the 47 bodies inside. “We will come back when more bodies come in,” Pariyar says. “I don’t know what I will do if I find him.”

Advertisement

The first thing confronting searching relatives is the smell, an utterly overwhelming mix of decomposition and disinfectant. Next, they must pore through A4 sheets of paper, stapled into a booklet, containing the forensic photos of bodies presently being processed. Police in Kathmandu unload bodies of people killed in the flood. KATE GERAGHTY Officials work to identify bodies at the Maharajgunj Medical Campus. KATE GERAGHTY Such photos are also posted on a wall across the road. Most images on both wall and in booklet are of figures so mangled by the flood and bloated from days in the sun and mud that it is difficult to see how any of them may be identified this way.

Advertisement

An official at the morgue says 24 have been identified since last week, though none yet on Friday. Related Article Floods In Nepal, hope gives way to grief. Few are counting on miracles The volume of death is so great for Nepal’s limited resources that bodies lie exposed. We travelled by chance behind a police bus ferrying bodies on Thursday afternoon, and see it again, parked at the morgue, close to 24 hours later with what an official confirms are some of the same bodies (and two rice sacks full of body parts) only now being unloaded. Seven Australian Federal Police identification specialists are due to arrive in Kathmandu at the weekend, adding to a 15-member disaster assistance response team that landed on Friday. A short walk away, people are giving samples of their DNA in the hope they may be able to retrieve family members from the mass graves, and afford them proper Hindu or Buddhist cremation.

Advertisement

The precinct at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital also contains the great wall of grief, on which relatives attach posters of their missing. When we visited soon after the disaster, the wall contained a couple of dozen posters. Now, there are hundreds, with more still being added. School boy Bibek Pariyar, on short post-exam break, has taken on the responsibility of helping people stick on their posters and fixing the ones coming undone. title: The West’s breathless AI spending spree can end only one way
text:
Advertisement

MoneyInvestingAI Opinion The West’s breathless AI spending spree can end only one way

Jeremy Warner September 5, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

But this time is different, right? As every student of investment trends knows, any boom will ultimately culminate in a bust. Yet almost invariably this truism – repeatedly proven by historical experience – is forgotten in the excitement of the boom du jour; or, rather, investors come to believe that in their particular case, the boom is perfectly sustainable. I do know a bubble when I see one, and the current breathless pace of investment in AI is undoubtedly that. iStock Equally invariably, belief in “this time is different” turns out to be flawed. As indeed it will be with the latest technological revolution to engulf the world of commerce: artificial intelligence. I have to confess to being somewhat bewildered by the pace, scale and complexity of the change that AI is bringing about, and readily admit to lacking the expertise to fully understand both the technology and its path to monetisation. I should add that this is not for want of trying.

Advertisement

But I do know a bubble when I see one, and the current breathless pace of investment in AI is undoubtedly that. It’s happening far too fast for the capital markets and the public to accommodate without mishap. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump is clutching at straws and the world knows it Ah, yes, but actually, say its cheerleaders, it is not nearly as big as some of those seen in the past; and unlike the dotcom boom of the late 1990s, or the British railway mania of the 1840s, it is substantially funded by the existing cash flows of the major tech giants. Both these observations are supported by the facts. At its peak, annual capital spending on railways reached an astonishing 20 per cent of British GDP, and even the investment boom in broadband supporting infrastructure during the 1990s reached close to 2 per cent of US GDP. Current data centre and associated hardware spending is “only” about 1.5 per cent of US GDP, and this is largely being met from the already burgeoning profits of “big tech”. All the same, the suspicion that what we are witnessing is another giant misallocation of capital refuses to go away.

Advertisement

Extreme levels of share price volatility among leading AI operatives already point to a basic, underlying lack of confidence in the highfalutin claims made for the earnings potential of this massive increase in capital spending. Up like a rocket in initial trading after its IPO a couple of months ago, then down like a spent stick, shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX now trade 17 per cent below the peak they reached shortly after the issue price. News that the company plans to double down on investment in computing power went down badly with investors. They thought they were investing in a rocket company, not another data centre behemoth. Elon Musk at the SpaceX debut. Bloomberg Lately, even the so-called “picks and shovels” trade – the notion that the real money in any gold rush is to be made not by the prospectors themselves but by those selling them the enabling hardware, in this case high-end processing and memory chips – has come off the boil in anticipation of an eventual pronounced slowdown in demand.

Advertisement

So far, there is still no sign of this in announced spending plans, but it doesn’t entirely quell fears of a sudden stop when investors and credit markets abruptly turn off the taps. A number of recent developments have added to these concerns. First and perhaps most important is the advent of our old friend, growing Chinese competition. This first became apparent with the launch in January last year of the Hangzhou-based DeepSeek, said to have been developed at a fraction of the cost of US frontier models but with equally powerful capabilities. Since then, there has been a steady stream of cheap and cheerful launches from China’s AI sector, including Alibaba’s Qwen 3.8 Max, which is said to be better in some respects than Anthropic’s flagship Fable 5. Before that, we’d seen the launch of Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, again said to be as good as many pricier Western models. Already, these Chinese upstarts are beginning to make significant inroads into Western markets, where their open-source approach to AI is thought perfectly adequate and in some ways better for most needs. Sound familiar? Yes, it follows exactly the same pattern as virtually every industry you care to think of. So much for “first-mover advantage”. In this case, as in many others, it is those slipstreaming in the wake of the pioneers that may reap the bigger harvest.

Advertisement

Not that this has in any way lessened the appetite among US hyperscalers for AI infrastructure investment. The US already has 5400 operational data centres, with many more planned. China, by contrast, has fewer than 500, though they tend to be bigger in scale. Related Article Mergers & acquisitions French trio minted as billionaires as the world’s most valuable company swoops In other words, China seems to be managing the AI transition on much smaller capital outlays than the US and Europe, thereby limiting the squeeze in overall capital spending that the AI leviathan inflicts on other industries and the fallout that might ensue from any slowdown in AI deployment. In the West, there is a real danger of AI becoming a kind of all-consuming black hole that sucks the life out of all other forms of investment. The other factor that should concern investors and lenders is the increasingly vocal public backlash against AI, manifested in sometimes violent local opposition to the construction of more data centres.

Advertisement

This is something quite new to America, which generally has a more positive attitude to cutting-edge industrial development than most other Western economies, and it seems to be directly linked not just to the appalling aesthetics and energy-guzzling characteristics of data centres but to a genuine loathing of the power of the tech giants and what they represent. Small-town America is not taking kindly to the tech bros of Silicon Valley remaking the world in their own image. Even Donald Trump, spooked by the growing number of cybersecurity incidents associated with OpenAI and Anthropic models, has begun to take note, though he qualifies support for more public control with the greater priority of winning the AI arms race with China. “We don’t want to restrict them where all of a sudden we come in second to China,” the US president said last week. “Whoever wins with AI is going to win. That’s how big it is ... I don’t want to restrict them from doing great work.” So the “great work” continues, turbocharged by China snapping at Silicon Valley’s heels. Those paying attention can only sit back and wonder how long this game of beggar-thy-neighbour can continue before cold reality bites.

Advertisement

It’s only just begun, say uber-bulls, pointing to plans for Google to supply Anthropic with more than $US150 billion ($208 billion) in AI chips. The fact that the Google-Anthropic deal relies on a complex “you scratch my back and I’ll scratch yours” money-go-round – always a bad sign – doesn’t seem to bother them. As long as the music is playing, you’ve got to get up and dance, said the chairman of Citigroup just ahead of the global financial crisis. Quite so. A plan to install a life-saving medicine dispenser near Melbourne’s safe injecting room has been scrapped after the local mayor claimed it would encourage drug use on the street rather than inside the medically supervised centre. The Victorian government is investigating locations for a free naloxone dispensing machine in the City of Yarra, as part of a statewide trial to make the vital medication – which can temporarily reverse an opioid overdose – more accessible. A free naloxone dispensing machine that’s been installed at the Alfred Hospital Emergency and Trauma Centre in Melbourne. Ruby Alexander Yarra Mayor Stephen Jolly wrote a letter to Health Minister Ingrid Stitt in June, asking her not to install a dispenser at a proposed site on Victoria Street near the North Richmond medically supervised injecting room. Yarra staff told councillors that Jolly’s letter and a subsequent meeting between the council and the Department of Health is ultimately why the location on Victoria Street is no longer being considered.

The mayor told The Age that while he would support a naloxone machine on-site at the safe injecting room or at the nearby St Vincent’s Hospital, he did not want it along such a major thoroughfare. “If we put [a machine] on Victoria Street … we’re encouraging people to use drugs on Victoria Street rather than go 100 metres to the south to the supervised injecting facility,” Jolly said. “When you whack [a machine] on Victoria Street, where all the locals are and all the traders are … it’s almost like rubbing their nose in it.” In June, the Victorian government announced a statewide trial program of the free 24/7 naloxone machines. Twenty dispensers will be rolled out as part of a wider $95 million program – 10 in Melbourne and 10 in regional Victoria. They will remain in place until June 2027.

Half of the machines have already been installed as part of the trial. A further seven local government areas have been earmarked as locations for the second tranche, but exact locations are yet to be announced. There are still plans to install a machine somewhere in Yarra. A government spokesperson did not answer questions about the specific location, when it would be installed, or whether the letter from Jolly had impacted any decisions. They said that discussions with the council to identify a suitable site commenced in August 2025. President of the Victoria Street Business Association Ha Nguyen said that although traders were supportive of naloxone and other life-saving measures, North Richmond was not the right place for a dispenser.

Amanda Stone, executive officer at the Yarra Drug and Health Forum and a former Yarra mayor, said polarising and politicised views around the safe injecting room have made it difficult to engage in constructive dialogue within the community.

title: Australian drone team arrives in Nepal as search for missing continues
text:
Australian drone operators have arrived in Nepal to help search for those missing in the country's disaster-stricken regions.

The 15-person specialist team landed in the capital late Friday, with additional support, including victim identification specialists on the way following a request for assistance from Nepali authorities.

A glacier collapse near Nepal's border with Tibet on 26 August triggered devastating floods across towns and valleys.

At least 36 Australians remain missing, with the federal government holding grave concerns for their welfare.

The death toll in Nepal is nearing 1300, with almost 4800 people still missing, including 601 foreign nationals, according to official figures released on Friday.

On the Tibetan side of the border, the death toll rose to 31 on Friday, an increase of 10 since the previous tally, according to Chinese state media.

It was not clear whether they were Chinese or foreign nationals. Some 531 people were reported missing, Reuters reports.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong confirmed on Thursday that local authorities would conduct searches in areas where many Australians were believed to have been staying.

She said Australian drone operators and incident management specialists would be sent to the region as part of a broader on-the-ground support team.

"I can indicate that after our inquiries that Nepali authorities have advised us that searches are being conducted in the locations identified by Australia, including (The Kailash Hotel) and the Royal Himalaya Hotel amongst others," Senator Wong told reporters.

The drone technology has AI capabilities that can help find victims, along with thermal imaging to identify anyone trapped.

DFAT is working with local authorities to establish the whereabouts and welfare of affected Australians and contact next of kin where appropriate.

Nepali authorities will also be given telecommunication data to help narrow the last known location of missing Australians.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers provided the latest update on the missing Australians on Friday, confirming that two more citizens were found safe.

It brings the number of Australians found since the catastrophic floods to seven, after five were confirmed safe on Wednesday.

Aid supplies aboard a Royal Australian Air Force plane also arrived in Kathmandu on Wednesday.

More than 1400 hygiene kits, 2200 solar lights and phone chargers were among the items.

title: The White House launched a video game. A major games company is not impressed
text:
In brief The White House has released a selection of video games in an attempt at youth outreach.

The games use copyrighted material from Sega and Xbox. One company is exploring legal options.

The company behind the long-running puzzle video game series Tetris has said that it did not give permission for the White House to use the game's iconic imagery for a controversial online arcade that the Trump administration released on Friday.

"The Tetris Company was not involved in the creation of ‘Build the Wall’ and did not authorise or license the Tetris brand or intellectual property for the game," Tetris told the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency in a statement.

"We are currently reviewing the matter," the statement continued.

A block-stacking game called Build the Wall included instructions to "protect the border from the coming horde."

The arcade-style games and promotional content used by the Trump administration contain images that resemble games created by Tetris and other major game developers, including Sega, Microsoft-owned Xbox and the Flappy Bird Foundation.

"At Tetris, we believe in the power of connection and bringing people together, not dividing them," Tetris said in a social media post.

"P.P.S. We take copyright infringement very seriously," the post continued.

Promotional content posted by the White House on social media also included images that resemble trademarks and designs from Microsoft-owned Xbox.

Microsoft did not respond to requests for comment, and the Sega Corporation couldn't immediately be reached.

The White House released several games Friday, with a placeholder that teased another one "coming soon."

The web-only games, which were published on the official White House website under a new page called "arcade," sparked condemnation for racist themes and prompted questions about potential copyright violations.

In one clip, the letters from the Sega logo transform into MAGA, a term that stands for Make America Great Again, which President Trump turned into his campaign slogan during his first presidential run for the 2016 election.

A game called "Flappy Bill" features a bald eagle carrying a document in its claws that tries to avoid smashing into columns of various heights, against a background that resembles Washington DC.

"This administration is laser focused on ways to innovate and tell the story of the President's many accomplishments in a way that resonates with every American," the White House said Thursday in a statement to AFP.

Rights groups criticised the White House.

"Makes me sick. They've been playing games with people's lives for years, now they've made a video game of what they're doing," Amerika Garcia Grewal, co-director of the Frontera Federation in Eagle Pass, Texas, told AFP.

"There's no attention paid to the quality of life for human beings, both those in their game or those in real life. We who live in the borderlands are US citizens and yet are treated with suspicion and violence," she added.

The game designers "have lost touch with what it means to be human and care for others."

Trump campaigned on a promise to expel millions of undocumented migrants and has taken several actions since returning to power aimed at speeding up deportations and reducing border crossings.

His White House meanwhile has long used social media stunts to ram home its points and troll liberal opponents, and has sparked a backlash from several artists by using their music without permission.

The White House is trying to convince voters that Trump's second presidential term has been successful ahead of the midterm election in November. The balance of power in Congress will also be at stake when Americans go to the polls in just over two months.

title: The UN has backed a new world map that makes Africa bigger and the US smaller
text:
In brief The UN has voted in favour of adopting a new world map.

The new map updates the centuries-old Mercator projection to a "more accurate" scale.

The United Nations General Assembly voted Saturday to back a resolution spearheaded by several African countries to adopt a map that makes their continent bigger while shrinking North America and Europe.

Aimed at "a more accurate representation" of continental landmasses, the resolution was supported by 164 countries while the United States voted against it and six other states abstained.

The new map — known as the Equal Earth cartographic projection — "is a relevant option for improving the accuracy of the cartographic representation of the world," the resolution said.

It urges member states to adopt the new map in place of the traditional Mercator projection, which was designed for maritime navigation by Flemish cartographer Gerardus Mercator in 1569.

Foreign Minister Robert Dussey of Togo, which drove the resolution, said maps "guide education, nourish the imagination, and influence collective perceptions."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"They are therefore never neutral, when they present a distorted image of our planet, they risk perpetuating inaccurate representation that are passed down through generation."

The United States, however, slammed the resolution, saying such moves are "the reason this institution is losing its credibility."

"Instead of focusing on genuine problems ... this body is debating map projects from the 16th century and their role in promoting reparations and cognitive justice," US representative Yaryna Ferencevych said ahead of the vote.

'Distorted representation'

The Mercator projection focused on accurate depictions of the shapes and angles of land masses, but their relative sizes were often inaccurate — in part due to the challenge of rendering a three-dimensional globe onto a two-dimensional map.

It inflated northern regions and compressed equatorial ones, making Europe and North America appear much larger, while shrinking Africa and South America.

A group of cartographers launched the Equal Earth projection in 2018. It makes Africa, Latin America, South Asia and Oceania appear much larger.

The Mercator projection has been the default map of the world since the 1500s, but it greatly distorts the size of many continents. Source: AAP / Mary Evans

"Equal Earth preserves the relative surface areas of continents and, as much as possible, shows their shapes as they appear on a globe," one of the cartographers, Bojan Savric, told the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency in 2025.

France — which co-sponsored the resolution in support of the new map — announced Saturday that it would abandon the Mercator projection.

In that map, "the United States, Russia and China take on a disproportionate visual prominence compared to Africa, Latin America or southeast Asia," while "Greenland appears almost as big as Africa," Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said.

"Changing maps obviously doesn't change the world," he said. "But correcting a distorted representation is already an act of truth."

The initiative comes as France is seeking to improve relations with Africa, particularly in former colonies with which it has prickly ties.

title: Why the 'great Aussie summer' may become a thing of the past
text:
Last summer, Paris Brooke watched in horror as a bushfire blazed through the national park across the lake from her township of Mallacoota in north-east Victoria.

The town wasn't directly at risk, but she knew what the impact would be.

"The camp park emptied out overnight, leaving businesses that depend on summer tourism stuck with unused supplies and staff, but no more tourists," Brooke tells SBS News.

The exodus was reminiscent of the summer of 2019-20, when Australia's Black Summer bushfires swept through and devastated the beachside town.

Mallacoota was among the hardest-hit areas. Apocalyptic-looking scenes of residents and holidaymakers sheltering in boats off the coast, under a red sky thick with smoke, were broadcast around the world.
