Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

While Brooke hasn't necessarily seen a slowdown in holidaymakers to the town since, she believes stays are shortening and worries the increased likelihood of extreme weather will hit summer trade long-term.

It's why she set up the Wilderness Collective, a community not-for-profit aimed at helping locals build new skills and businesses to reduce reliance on summer tourism.

"People are much more aware of natural disasters such as bushfires or droughts," she says.

Catastrophic fire conditions last summer burned through tens of thousands of hectares, destroyed multiple homes and other structures and forced widespread evacuations in central Victoria alone. Source: Getty / Jesse Thompson

On the same day last summer, climate scientist Linden Ashcroft was on the beach in Mallacoota. She recalls her kids playing in the water as embers and burnt leaves fell around them.

"It was pretty heartbreaking and terrifying. Everyone was really creeped out, and the town was covered in smoke," she says.

It left her with a lasting sense of cognitive dissonance — this is not how summer is supposed to feel.

That feeling is now rippling around the country, reaching far beyond places like Mallacoota that are historically prone to bushfires.

"Black Summer 2019–2020 was a real step change; it made people face the reality that summer can't just be carefree anymore," Ashcroft says.

You could call it the end of summer as we know it — or an evolution.

Climate Council director and academic Lesley Hughes says the changing climate is reshaping Australians' notion of summer: instead of looking forward to it, people increasingly feel apprehensive.

"They dread the heatwaves, the bushfires, not being able to do the things they used to. Climate change is stealing the part of the year Australians looked forward to most."

With higher temperatures and more extreme weather events becoming a fixture of the holiday season in parts of the country, could this signal the end of 'great Aussie summer'?

How our summers are changing

Australia is now 1.5C warmer on average than it was a century ago, according to the National Climate Risk Assessment. It's driving more extreme heatwaves and dangerous fire weather.

Monash climate scientist Andrew Watkins, former head of the Bureau of Meteorology's long-range forecast team, says the expected shifts will likely be dramatic.

"Heatwaves will cover larger areas, happen more frequently and grow more intense, with longer fire seasons stretching into autumn and spring. Rainfall will be less frequent but more intense, raising flash flood risk. Tropical cyclones may become less frequent but more severe," he tells SBS News.

Source: SBS News

Rising humidity is also driving up "wet-bulb temperature" — a combined heat-and-humidity measure that determines how well sweat can cool the body. Watkins says high readings — when sweat stops evaporating because the humidity is too high — put children and the elderly at particular risk.

"The temperature might only be 35, but if the wet-bulb is up to 25, you're going to put your body under a huge amount of stress."

Looking ahead to this summer, the Bureau of Meteorology has forecast a strong El Niño — generally meaning hotter, drier conditions — which it expects will mainly affect parts of Australia's east and south-east, raising the risk of drought and bushfires.

As extreme heat becomes more commonplace in Australia, other countries face similar conditions. Los Angeles was hit by raging wildfires last January, and Europe endured one of its worst summers on record for fire and heat this year.

It's a trend that is unlikely to shift without major and rapid structural changes, shifting global energy use to renewables and divesting from fossil fuels to limit further global warming.

New data published this week by the UN Environment Programme showed the world has lost the fight to limit warming to 1.5C. Even the most optimistic projections now point to warming of at least 1.8C — locking in more extreme weather, ecosystem loss and sea-level rise.

Reorganising the year

As projections worsen, experts are turning their attention to health risks.

Hughes at the Climate Council says the impacts of excess heat on the body can creep up slowly, and are especially dangerous for the elderly, the young, and those with heart or respiratory conditions.

She suggests more public awareness of the risks associated with heat stress is needed, but she's also calling for something more radical: reframing the calendar year to keep more of us inside during the country's hottest months.

Maybe a lot of summer would be better spent indoors, in air-conditioning, working, and leisure time moved to spring and autumn.

"Maybe our biggest school holidays shouldn't be in January," she says, adding "that would be an enormous social change for Australia".

Not everyone can escape the heat during their workday either. Professions such as tradies, farmhands, park rangers, delivery riders and some hospitality and event workers, for example, have no choice but to endure it.

A Spanish study published in 2023 offers another perspective, instead proposing to shift the country's national holidays to align with its hottest weeks to boost productivity and reduce industrial electricity consumption. Researchers found moving Spain's traditional holiday period from August to late July — the point of peak heat damage — would cut heat-driven electricity demand by 3 per cent, lost work hours by 25 per cent, and ozone pollution by 4 per cent.

Source: SBS News

Whether holidaying or working over summer, the general advice is to find ways to stay cool, and limit outdoor time to early mornings or evenings.

Although now, some Australians are reconsidering how they spend the season altogether.

The rise of the 'coolcation'

Research suggests people are already adapting to climate change without realising it, as evidenced by the rise in 'coolcations' — holidays to cool-climate destinations.

For Australians, this might include escapes to parts of northern Europe instead of southern Europe; visiting the tropics in winter instead of summer; venturing south to New Zealand or Tasmania for a mid-summer break; or snowy escapes to the Arctic, Antarctica or Alpine villages.

Trip.com data shows a 74 per cent year-on-year jump in searches for cooler destinations since the start of 2026, spiking 237 per cent across the June–August northern hemisphere summer. Searches for flights to Iceland rose 85 per cent, as travellers favoured northern Europe over traditionally popular Mediterranean spots. In Asia, cooler destinations such as Inner Mongolia, Yunnan in China and Sapporo in Japan saw similar gains.

Cold-climate destinations like Lapland in northern Scandinavia are becoming more popular, with more people seeking fun in the cold. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

Holidaygoers are also increasingly considering extreme weather events when making travel plans. Booking.com's 2026 Travel & Sustainability Report found 74 per cent of travellers now factor extreme weather into where and when they travel, and 31 per cent have cancelled a trip because of it.

In Australia, the Climate Council found 61 per cent of people are concerned about extreme weather disrupting summer holidays and are adapting — shifting from inland bush locations to the coast or travelling in cooler months.

Climate scientist Watkins is a coolcationer and spends his summers camping in Victoria's cooler high country.

"[It's about] beach holidays in spring, camping in autumn, taking more advantage of Easter. Getting up into cooler places over summer is a joy."

Travelling in cooler months isn't just about comfort, of course; it often also means fewer crowds and protecting destinations from over-tourism in mid-summer.

If you're holidaying in summer

However, travelling to far-flung places to access cooler weather may not be viable for some people. Distance and cost can be prohibitive, even for domestic travel.

Simply avoiding regional or bushfire-prone areas isn't necessarily a silver bullet either.

Ashcroft warns that heat risk in major cities can be just as dangerous.

"Urban areas get hotter due to the heat-island effect, so vulnerable people may not be better off in cities."

Australia's summers on the whole are becoming hotter, drier and more intense. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

No matter where you spend the summer months, the advice is familiar by now: watch the forecasts, have a fire or heat plan, know when to leave early if conditions turn catastrophic, and avoid driving through floodwaters or bushfire smoke, which can be as thick as fog. Sometimes that means a detour, or staying put overnight until the danger passes.

Ashcroft thinks the language around summer should change altogether to help people prepare and understand the risks.

"Seasons are baked into how we talk about our year, but they're changing, so the way we talk about them has to change too. The Bureau's new term 'severe weather season' is more honest," she says.

"Being real helps us plan and prepare."

Rethinking summer sport

As our summers become more brutal, outdoor events such as music festivals and sport events may also become more challenging.

Ashcroft questions whether it still makes sense to push elite athletes to compete in extreme heat, conditions that are "not healthy and not safe".

Joanne Bowen is CEO of Cricket for Climate, a player-led movement that aims to build resilience for community clubs and the game. She calls cricket "the canary in the coal mine" for how climate change is disrupting outdoor activities.

Grassroots clubs are already cancelling junior games on hot days, with many lacking the infrastructure and budgets to adequately light night matches.

A bone dry cricket field in Bray, England, which like much of the country experienced prolonged dry weather and extreme heat this past summer. Source: Getty / Dan Kitwood

At the elite level, players have also struggled to perform in the heat, adds Bowen.

"But it's not just about the players; fans in concrete stadiums are exposed as well."

Increasing rainfall during summer is a growing problem too, she adds.

"If there's rain, you simply can't play, and there are commercial consequences for partners and fans."

She expects more games to move to nighttime and says shifting the cricket season to winter or spring is possible, though it would clash with other codes.

Another staple of Australian summer is the Australian Open.

Tennis Australia declined to discuss the long-term viability of tennis as a summer sport or moving the Australian Open from its midsummer slot, but a spokesperson said in a statement the organisation "continues to introduce strategies to protect the safety of players in hot conditions".

These include shading, misting fans, science-based heat guidelines with real-time monitoring, and heat acclimatisation education for players arriving from overseas.

The organisation's response to heat also appears to be shifting. Back in 2014, tournament director Craig Tiley defended playing through 40C conditions, saying "we are, at the end of the day, an outdoor event", even as players required medical attention.

By contrast, this year organisers suspended play after defending champion Jannik Sinner cramped mid-match under 40C conditions, with play resuming under a closed roof.

Italian tennis player Jannik Sinner recovers from heat stress during the Australian Open in January 2026. Source: AAP / Dita Alangkara/AP

Planning for future summers

Beyond the challenge of adjusting our summer holiday plans to increasingly extreme weather, a deeper issue persists: how to curb climate change.

The best way to protect Australian summers, experts say, is to stop burning fossil fuels.

"We have to address the root cause of the problem, and Australia has a big responsibility to do that," says the Climate Council's Hughes.

Experts say adaptation can't wait: retrofitting homes with renewable energy, better resourcing emergency services and warning systems, investing in coastal protection, and upgrading infrastructure — from power grids to more public cooling and green spaces — all matter now more than ever.

Climate scientist Watkins wants to see more rigorous climate risk assessments underpin a genuine national adaptation plan, backed by coordination across all levels of government.

"The most important thing is coordinated efforts — talking with communities, business sectors, and the public to find out locally what adaptation is possible," he says.

I think we'll still have fun [in summer]. We'll just need to do things a little differently.

Back in Mallacoota, Brooke’s Wilderness Collective is helping locals to build off-season opportunities.

"We're working hard to broaden the economy, so visitors come throughout the year. Winter is actually the best time to visit; it's less crowded and the weather's beautiful," she says.

"We're starting to see visitors spread across the year, which is great, but we need more of it."

Even as Australians adapt to the new realities of summer, a trade-off is occurring.

For Watkins, adapting also means facing loss.

"There's a kind of grief that doesn't get talked about enough — grief for a place," he says.

"Many of us return to the same spots every summer, hoping our kids will see them the way we first did. But those places are changing. The National Climate Risk Assessment confirms it: huge numbers of plant and animal species are already shifting, with more change ahead.

"That sense of loss is real, and it deserves to be taken seriously."

title: This virus has evolved. Australia doesn't have a new vaccine
text:
IN BRIEF Pfizer's latest COVID vaccine targets the XFG subvariant, but it has not yet been registered for use in Australia.

Experts say Australia's vaccine update process could be streamlined as new COVID variants continue to emerge.

Australians can't yet access a COVID-19 vaccine tailored for new variants, highlighting how Australia's system tends to lag behind, as a major manufacturer confirms it has no plans to push into Australia's market.

Pfizer and BioNTech's latest COVID-19 vaccine, adapted to target the XFG subvariant, has been approved in the United States for the 2026-27 season, following international guidance to more closely match vaccines with contemporary circulating variants.

Australia does not yet have that formulation registered.

But experts say the lag is not necessarily cause for alarm, with Australia continuing to monitor circulating variants and having access to relatively recent updated vaccines.

Pfizer and BioNTech's LP.8.1-adapted COVID-19 vaccine was registered on the Australian Register of Therapeutic Goods in late 2025 and became available in Australia in December.

Moderna's LP.8.1 formulation has also been registered in Australia.

Australia has updated vaccines — just not the latest formulation

The issue is therefore less about Australia going without updated COVID-19 vaccines, and more about how quickly newer formulations can be made available as the virus continues to evolve.

Professor Paul Griffin, an infectious diseases physician and clinical microbiologist, said Australia tended to lag behind some countries in updating COVID-19 vaccines.

"I think it's just some of the way we're managing those updates just means it's not quite happening as streamlined a way as we might like," he said.

"We know that some countries are able to do that a bit more quickly."

Griffin said countries with more established frameworks could update vaccines closer to real time.

"We tend to lag behind a little bit," he said.

While he said faster access would be preferable, he also stressed the importance of continuing to update vaccines as the virus changes.

Several reasons for the delay

But Sarah McGuinness, a senior research fellow at Monash University, told SBS News there was no single explanation for why a new formulation might become available overseas before it does in Australia.

She said one factor is the decisions vaccine manufacturers make about which countries to seek regulatory approval in, and when, with vaccine sponsors responsible for deciding whether to seek regulatory approval in different countries.

McGuinness also said Australia is a relatively small market compared with areas such as the US and Europe, meaning new formulations are not always brought here first.

Peter Markey, a GP and public health physician who chairs the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners' public health special interest group, said Australian authorities were continuing to monitor the virus internationally.

He said governments, researchers and the World Health Organization would be watching circulating strains and sub-strains and "looking out for vaccines to match them".

There is also an established international process for determining which variants vaccines should target.

Pfizer and BioNTech say their latest XFG-adapted vaccine follows guidance to more closely match contemporary circulating variants.

Along with Pfizer-BioNTech's XFG-adapted vaccine, updated vaccines from Moderna and Novavax-Sanofi have been approved in the US for the 2026-27 season.

AstraZeneca has confirmed to SBS News that it has no plans to release a COVID-19 vaccine for the 2026-27 season.

It withdrew its vaccine from the global market in 2024, and it hadn't been available in Australia since 2023.

What does the lag mean for Australians?

For Australians, the emergence of newer formulations overseas does not mean the vaccines currently available are ineffective.

The challenge is keeping vaccine formulations aligned with a virus that continues to evolve.

Pfizer confirmed to SBS News that its LP.8.1-adapted vaccine is registered in Australia and available to people aged six months and older.

The company has not provided a timeframe for when its newer XFG-adapted vaccine could be submitted for Australian registration.

Griffin said Australia could nevertheless look for ways to streamline the updating process.

"I think that's just where we need to consider a really streamlined way of getting those updated vaccines here and available in Australia as quickly as possible," he said.

For now, experts say Australia's vaccine system is continuing to monitor the changing virus, while manufacturers decide which updated formulations to bring to the Australian market.

title: 'Beneath their office': Why the US-Canada dispute has turned so nasty
text:
IN BRIEF Trade talks between the US and Canada collapsed last month after Canada rejected what it called unacceptable US demands.

Donald Trump has escalated the dispute with tariffs, personal attacks and repeated suggestions Canada should become a US state.

What began as a trade fight between two of the world's most closely connected economies has escalated into a broader confrontation over Canada's sovereignty, culture and military, with United States President Donald Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney now trading increasingly personal attacks.

The latest escalation follows the collapse of trade talks between the two countries on 21 August.

Canada walked away from negotiations after saying the US had made unacceptable last-minute demands, while the US has argued there was a deal on the table that Canada chose not to accept.

The US has since imposed 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars of Canadian goods, with Canada preparing retaliatory measures of its own.

Since then, the dispute has spilled well beyond trade. Trump has repeatedly suggested Canada should become the 51st US state, ordered US federal agencies to refer to Lake Ontario as "Lake America" and continued to attack Canadian leaders online.

US officials have also mocked Canada's military, prompting Carney to accuse Washington of "doing memes", "throwing shade" and "trying to be tough".

But beneath the memes and insults is a serious economic standoff that both sides still say could ultimately be resolved at the negotiating table.

Origins of the feud

While Trump has imposed 50 per cent tariffs on about US$20 billion ($27 billion) worth of Canadian goods, Canada is preparing retaliatory tariffs of roughly the same value on US products from 8 September.

But the disagreement isn't just about tariffs.

Carney says the US was seeking terms that would have left major Canadian industries, particularly the highly integrated auto sector, effectively operating as subsidiaries of US companies.

He has also accused the US of seeking changes that would affect Canada's French-language and cultural protections, as well as restrictions on Canada's ability to negotiate future free trade agreements with other countries.

Canada has rejected those demands as a threat to its economic interests and sovereignty.

The Trump administration disputes Canada's account of the negotiations and has argued that a deal was available that Canada chose not to accept.

Why has sovereignty become such a big issue?

Trump has repeatedly suggested that Canada should become the 51st US state, a proposal Canada has firmly rejected.

What might once have sounded like political provocation has become a central part of the dispute, with Carney increasingly framing the confrontation as a defence of Canadian sovereignty.

That rhetoric carries particular weight in Quebec, where there are concerns about what US absorption of Canada could mean for the province's French language and culture.

Carney has also pushed back against any suggestion that the US should have a say over who Canada trades with.

"Canada is a sovereign state," he said.

"We will strike free trade deals with the countries we wish to strike free trade deals with."

Why is the rhetoric getting so personal?

Since the trade talks collapsed, Trump has repeatedly attacked Canada's leadership and used social media to taunt the country.

He has described Canada's leaders as among the worst he has to deal with, and posted an AI-generated meme depicting Canadian geese with his distinctive hairstyle marching under a US flag.

US defence secretary Pete Hegseth appeared to take aim at Canada's military, posting an image of two female Canadian military cadets training in British Columbia with the words "this is real" alongside a Canadian flag.

US treasury secretary Scott Bessent also mocked Canada's military, later saying that Carney had received a "verbal beatdown" from him and Hegseth.

Carney said the comments from members of Trump's administration were "beneath their office".

"When the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade and stop trying to be tough, and start being serious about having those discussions, we can have those discussions," Carney said.

Why does it matter beyond the insults?

The US and Canada have one of the world's most deeply integrated economic relationships.

That means prolonged disruption could affect workers, businesses and consumers on both sides of the border, particularly in industries such as manufacturing and autos, where supply chains frequently cross the border.

The Canadian government has warned that it cannot accept an agreement that it believes would weaken its domestic industries or limit its ability to make its own economic decisions.

At the same time, Carney has stressed that Canada is not looking for a permanent economic rupture with its largest trading partner.

On Thursday, he said Canada was ready to sign a deal with the US if it benefited both countries and provided "stability and credibility".

He also suggested there had been a recent softening in Washington's position.

Carney said the US had been pushing certain demands around Canadian language and culture right up until the talks collapsed, but was no longer insisting on them.

"Now, they're not," he said. "Well, if they didn't care, they shouldn't have kept them in the deal."

Is a deal still possible?

Despite the increasingly bitter rhetoric, Carney says the door to negotiations remains open.

He has repeatedly said Canada is prepared to return to the table when the US is ready to have serious discussions.

Trump's response has been less conciliatory.

After Carney's comments on Thursday, Trump posted that it was "very good for Canadian Politicians like Prime Minister Mark Carney to make President Donald J. Trump 'the enemy.'"

He warned that Canada's economy could collapse and be "worse than anything that has ever happened to a Canadian politician".

So while the memes, insults and threats have grabbed the headlines, the underlying dispute remains fundamentally about power.

Canada is trying to protect its industries and preserve its ability to make independent economic and cultural decisions.

Trump's administration is pushing for a trade relationship on terms more favourable to the US.

And both sides are now testing how far they are willing to go, without completely severing a relationship that neither country can easily walk away from.

title: Argentine president reignites Falklands dispute after Trump questions UK sovereignty
text:
In brief Argentine President Javier Milei has reignited a dispute with the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands.

It comes after US President Donald Trump said the US would reconsider its neutral stance on the islands' sovereignty.

Argentine President Javier Milei escalated his country's long-running dispute with the United Kingdom over the Falkland Islands, praising US President Donald Trump for saying the US could reconsider its historically neutral stance on the islands' sovereignty.

In a nationally televised address on Thursday night local time, Milei seized on Trump's comments this week that the US could review its position on the islands, casting the potential shift as proof that his close relationship with the US president — often criticised by political opponents — was paying dividends.

"The United States is considering this change in position because it knows that Argentina has a reliable partner, aligned with Western values, in a strategically important position that can be a valuable ally in the decades to come," Milei said.

The libertarian Argentine leader then announced a series of actions aimed at stopping the development of the Sea Lion oil project, about 220km north of the islands, where UK company Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum plan to begin drilling in the coming months and start producing oil in 2028.

Argentina considers the project an illegal exploitation of resources in waters it claims as its own.

He threatened tougher sanctions against companies involved in offshore drilling and announced new funding for a naval base in Argentina's southernmost province, Tierra del Fuego, to bolster the country's military presence near the islands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas.

"Argentina will not stand idly by," Milei said. "Any further advance on the Malvinas Islands will be considered a violation of our national security."

READ MORE Argentina faces FIFA fine after players celebrate win against England with Falklands banner

Milei's effort to refocus national attention on the Falklands marks a striking turn for a leader who has faced criticism at home for warming ties with the UK and professing admiration for Margaret Thatcher, the UK prime minister who led the country to retake the remote archipelago during the 1982 Falklands War after Argentina had invaded it.

The two-month conflict killed 649 Argentine troops, 255 British service members and three islanders.

The sovereignty claim remains one of the few causes that cuts across Argentina's stark political divides, giving Milei a welcome political opening as his approval ratings slip and the economy sputters.

"We can argue about my style. We can disagree over fiscal or exchange-rate policy," Milei said.

"But this issue demands that we lay down our arms and show a united front to the world as a nation and as a society. There are causes that rise above any political difference. The Malvinas is one of them."

Argentina maintains that it inherited sovereignty over the islands from its former coloniser, Spain, and that the UK has illegally occupied them since 1833. The UK rejects that claim, citing the islanders' desire to remain a British overseas territory.

Britain insisted that the Falkland Islands "are British" after Milei's comments.

"The Falklands are British because Falkland Islanders choose to be British," British defence secretary Wes Streeting responded in a social media post on Friday.

"Our commitment to the Falklands is absolute and unshakeable," Streeting added.

Trump questions US support for British sovereignty

For decades, successive US administrations have remained neutral on the competing Argentine and UK sovereignty claims over the Falklands while recognising the UK's de facto administration of the islands. Any departure from that position would be a major diplomatic affront and inflame already high trans-Atlantic tensions.

On Monday, Trump fuelled frenzied speculation in the UK when asked whether his administration was reviewing its stance on the decades-old dispute.

"I always review every position," he replied. "That's just one of many."

Then, in an interview aired on Thursday with UK broadcaster GB News, Trump avoided directly answering a question about whether the US would "come to the aid" of the UK in another conflict over the Falklands.

The Falkland Islands have been under UK control for nearly 200 years. Credit: Supplied

Instead, he repeated past complaints that Britain had not provided sufficient support for the US-led bombing campaign against Iran.

"Your country was not there to help me," Trump said, recalling that the UK's former prime minister, Keir Starmer, told him the country did not have ships to contribute to the campaign.

"It was pretty sad, the whole thing."

The Trump administration has floated the Falklands as leverage before: An internal Pentagon email leaked in April first raised the prospect of the US reconsidering its position on the islands as one possible way to punish NATO allies that declined to join the US war on Iran.

In response, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham's spokesman, Tom Wells, said the British government's position was "long-standing and unwavering".

"Sovereignty rests with the UK, and the islanders' right to self-determination is paramount," Wells said earlier this week, pointing to a 2013 referendum in which the roughly 4,000 people living in the Falkland Islands voted overwhelmingly in favour of remaining a British overseas territory.

title: Feminist icon Gloria Steinem remembered as a 'fearless trailblazer' after death at 92
text:
In brief US feminist icon Gloria Steinem has died at the age of 92.

Tributes have poured in from around the world, with Nancy Pelosi describing her as a "fearless trailblazer".

Tributes have poured in after Gloria Steinem, the United States journalist, author and activist who was one of the most recognisable and enduring faces of the feminist movement, died at age 92.

In a statement on Thursday, Steinem's foundation announced: "Yesterday, Gloria Steinem passed away peacefully at her home in New York City, surrounded by some of the many who loved her."

Her death has sparked tributes to her decades of boundary-pushing activism.

Hillary Clinton, the first woman to serve as US secretary of state and the first female US presidential nominee of a major political party, said Steinem "pushed open doors not just for herself, but for literally millions of women behind her".

Nancy Pelosi, the first woman to be US House speaker, called Steinem "a fearless trailblazer who transformed the fight for equality in America and inspired generations of women to know their power".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"She lit a torch many years ago. It is now our responsibility to keep it lifted into the future," tennis champion Billie Jean King, winner of the famed 1973 "Battle of the Sexes" match, said.

Before becoming a leading figure in the women's rights movement, Steinem cut her teeth in journalism in the 1960s, denouncing the inequalities women in the US endured at a time when many needed their husband's approval to open a bank account.

She came to prominence in 1963 with an exposé of the pervasive sexism faced by cocktail waitresses at New York's Playboy Club.

But she credited her awakening to activism to a 1969 meeting where women described the ordeal of having an abortion.

"It made some sense of my own experience. I had had an abortion and had never told anyone," she later recounted in an article in New York Magazine.

The London doctor who gave her an abortion in 1957, when it was still illegal, made her promise two things: "First, you will not tell anyone my name. Second, you will do what you want to do with your life."

In the 1970s, she founded Ms Magazine and the National Women's Political Caucus and organised the first National Women's Conference in Houston.

Gloria Steinem rose to prominence in the 1960s with an exposé on the sexism faced by cocktail waitresses at New York's Playboy Club. Source: Getty / Bettye Lane / Photo Researchers History

Donning her trademark aviator glasses, Steinem headlined conferences and protests in the US and around the world for decades. She remained an outspoken defender of women's rights well into her later years.

When in 2022 the US Supreme Court overturned the Roe v Wade decision of 1973, which had enshrined the right to abortion, she pointed out: "Banning abortions does not stop the need for them. It just bans their safety.

"Don't agonise. Organise," she urged.

After a lifetime battling injustice, she told Agence France-Presse in 2019: "I think the role of older people like me is to have hope, because we remember when it was worse."

Public scrutiny

Born in Ohio on 25 March 1934, Steinem had a nomadic childhood with a travelling salesman father.

Her parents divorced when she was 10, forcing her to care for her mother, who had mental health issues.

As a frontline feminist, she came under intense scrutiny from both sides of the political spectrum.

Her good looks, miniskirts and brief experience as a Playboy Bunny were used against her in attempts to undermine her credibility.

READ MORE Julia Gillard says 'manosphere' requires new approach to gender equality

The fact that she remained single and childless was also weaponised.

At 66, she married businessman David Bale, the father of actor Christian Bale.

Asked by a reporter why she had changed her position on single life, she said: "I didn't change. Marriage changed."

Bale died three years later of brain cancer, aged 62. Steinem herself underwent surgery for breast cancer in the 1980s.

Second-wave feminist leader

Some younger activists saw Steinem — a leader of second-wave feminism from the 1960s to 1980s, which challenged job discrimination, reproductive rights and cultural sexism — as representing an outdated type of feminism.

She was criticised for defending Bill Clinton in 1989 when the then-governor of Arkansas was accused of sexual harassment.

In 2016, when Clinton's wife, Hillary, was vying to become the first female president in US history but struggling to garner support among women, Steinem suggested that young women preferred her rival, Bernie Sanders, because young men liked him.

"When you're young, you're thinking: 'Where are the boys? The boys are with Bernie,'" she told talk show host Bill Maher. She later apologised.

Steinem was given numerous awards and honours, including the US Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2013.

Supporters stopped outside Steinem's Manhattan apartment on Thursday to pay respects.

"I'm just feeling very inspired and grateful for the life that she led," Makenna Lorange, 31, who was visiting from Boston, said.

"We've lost a little bit of light in the world... [I'm] feeling renewed inspiration to carry on the torch in my own small ways going forward."

title: Pacific leaders voice concern over Chinese missile test but stop short of condemnation
text:
In brief The Pacific Islands Forum has agreed to "register concern" over a Chinese missile test in July.

The statement falls short of condemnation, and Nauru dissented the clause.

The Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) has wrapped up with most nations agreeing to "register concern" on China's recent intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) test, "which overflew a number of members without adequate notice".

"Leaders call on all states undertaking ICBM testing to ensure transparency and reassurance, including through the provision of advance notification of a test at least 24 hours in accordance with international practice," the communique says, as read out by Palau's President and PIF chair Surangel Whipps Junior, after the closing ceremony.

But it was not unanimous.

In a rare move for the usually consensus-based forum, Nauru was the only one of 18 PIF members to dissent from the clause.

Kiribati and Nauru were the only two Pacific nations that had previously blocked a draft PIF statement in the immediate aftermath of Beijing's test, a move that Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had been advocating for.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

However the statement went further than analysts and government sources had expected; the PIF foreign ministers' meeting statement in August was broader, discussing ballistic missile testing in the region, but had stopped short of singling out a particular ICBM or referencing a notice period for nations to undergo any testing.

Whipps also hit back against China's comments that Palau sensationalised its ballistic missile test, saying: "There's no sensationalism, it's just stating the facts."

"The Pacific Islands weren't informed [of the test]. The ones that were informed were informed late, and so I think the message from the forum is clear: that transparency needs to happen."

Intelligence shows the nuclear-capable intercontinental ballistic missile test in July flew over the Philippines, Palau and Micronesia's airspace before landing in the Pacific Ocean.

Several nations had criticised the test, just the second since 1980.

The response has become something of a litmus test for PIF and its members for their strategic positioning.

READ MORE Albanese responds after China warns of 'consequences' over Taiwan at Pacific summit

The communique's relevant clause includes a reference to the Fiji-led Ocean of Peace declaration made last year, which states the region should be free from coercion and militarisation.

However, it doesn't name China, nor does it use heftier diplomatic language than "concern".

While Australian officials were happy with the agreed statement, it fell short of some pre-retreat expectations, including those of the host, Palau.

Whipps made his displeasure with the test clear, which followed a 2024 effort.

"They sent a missile next to French Polynesia, another one next to Tuvalu, crossing over our airspace. They never bothered to tell us that's what's happening," he said.

"I said 'there's a lot of space between Japan and Guam, why don't you send it there? Why does it have to come to the middle of the Pacific when last year we just signed a declaration of peace?'

"We don't want our backyard, our homes, to be threatened and really disrespected."

Whipps said "a unified Pacific voice" would be critical to get Beijing to "respect sovereignty".

No region-wide pact

In other decisions of the leaders' retreat, PIF will categorise external powers, currently known as "dialogue partners", as either strategic or sector partners.

The 13 strategic partners will be China, the US, France, Germany, the UK, the EU, Canada, Japan, India, Indonesia, Singapore, South Korea and the UAE.

Those partners will be able to continue to travel to leaders' meetings, while sector partners will be referred to the annual foreign ministers gathering.

A region-wide security pact, championed by Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale, did not progress — as expected, given Wale's absence.

A proposal to bring the Australia-backed Joint Heads of Pacific Security under the Pacific Islands Forum has also garnered some support.

title: 'Hard to continue': Harvey's future is in limbo as his sport faces an existential threat
text:
Ski resorts across Australia have faced one of the hottest winters on record. For Australian snowboarder Harvey Edmanson, this is a threat to his future, and to the future of young snow athletes across Australia.

Speaking to SBS, the member of the Australian Alpine Snowboard National Team said: "If I don't have snow and training opportunities in Australia, it's going to make it really hard to continue."

Many professional snow athletes, including Edmanson, are self-funded. He has to fit his training around working as a façade designer in Melbourne.

The 27-year-old does most of his training at Mount Buller in Victoria but also ventures further north to the Perisher and Thredbo resorts in NSW.

Typically, he aims to train on the slopes from early July until late September. This year his start was delayed by three weeks and he was forced to stop in late August.

"It makes it hard when I miss out on over a month of training," Edmanson said.

Additionally, to train at a high level, Edmanson and other athletes need a sectioned-off part of the slope where they can set up racing conditions.

READ MORE Australia’s winter wonderland is becoming increasingly reliant on a backup plan

Ski resorts are usually happy to accommodate this, but have found it harder this year due to having a smaller area with sufficient snow depth.

"When there's only limited snow and limited run hill space, then it's not possible," Edmanson said.

Australian snow athletes often compete overseas during the northern hemisphere’s winter before returning to train in Australia in the off-season.

As snow seasons get shorter, Edmanson said athletes are skipping Australia entirely and starting to look overseas for off-season training.

This is not something he can do given he needs to work, and he joked that he "can't commute to New Zealand".

Mount Buller is a popular snow sports destination north-east of Melbourne. Source: LightRocket / Ye Myo Khant

Will young athletes feel the consequences?

Some in the snow sports community fear for future generations of Australian snow athletes if opportunities continue to dwindle for younger athletes seeking to develop.

Edmanson runs a futures program for developing athletes and says there's a lot of young athletes who are "looking to compete, looking to train, and they don't get enough time on snow in Australia".

Many younger athletes need to balance school and practice. Edmanson didn’t travel overseas to compete until he finished school.

"The most important part of my training and development all happened in Australia," he said. "It's really scary that there's a lot of young athletes that might not have that opportunity."

This year’s Milano Cortina Winter Olympics provided an injection of optimism into Australian snow sports after the Australian team won a national best three golds, two silvers and one bronze.

To continue this momentum, Edmanson says we need to give young athletes "that opportunity from riding at home".

Australian athletes enjoyed a successful 2026 Milano Cortina Winter Olympics, including 15-year-old Indra Brown, who finished 5th in the halfpipe event. Source: AAP / Dan Himbrechts

What does the future hold for Australian snow?

Several factors contributed to this year’s historically short snow season. A spokesperson for the Bureau of Meteorology told SBS that: "Long periods with high pressure systems in the Tasman Sea occurred during winter, directing warmer air from the north over south-eastern Australia."

Dr Linden Ashcroft, a senior lecturer in climate science at the University of Melbourne, told SBS: "we just didn't get the big cold fronts, the big Antarctic blasts of cold air, as often this winter".

Not every year will be as light on snow as this year, experts say, but broader trends are concerning.

READ MORE Australia’s winter wonderland is becoming increasingly reliant on a backup plan

Also speaking to SBS, the University of Canberra’s Duanne White, associate professor in ecology and genomics, said: "there's a lot of things that go into determining how much snow we have in the mountains in any particular one year", however: "the trend is obvious".

These conditions are likely to deteriorate over the coming years, with Ashcroft saying: "We already know that next year is going to be the world's hottest on record."

"We have already locked into not having snow seasons like the seasons that maybe our parents had."

Is it too late for snow sports in Australia?

Snowboarding and downhill skiing require around 30cm of snow. Resorts must maintain this level of snow for at least 60 days a year to remain economically viable.

The use of snowmaking machines has become necessary for many resorts. But these also require cold temperatures to operate.

White explained that resorts "generate snow in a factory, effectively on site with a giant freezer, and then blow that onto the slopes," but added that "that's not exactly sustainable for a broad scale".

Perisher is among Australia's snow sports destinations facing challenges from the changing climate. Credit: Andy Kirkwood

Despite the downward trend, Ashcroft said: "It's never too late. It's never too late to stop making things get worse." Edmanson echoed this saying: "No, there's steps [people can take]".

Edmanson works with Protect Our Winters (POW), an organisation made up of climate scientists and advocates, that seeks to protect cold weather in Australia.

Modelling from POW predicts that under a "low emission scenario" Australian snow sports could still have a strong future. To reach this scenario, the organisation advocates for a "transition away from fossil fuels".

Ashcroft said: "It's not too late to save the snow, but we have to act now, and we have to act fast." However he said we "need to prepare for a future that doesn't look like the past".

Edmandon said he hopes the "next generation have the same opportunities that I do, that I had when I was a developing athlete".

"Being in the Australian Alps, is an incredible environment. It's super beautiful, and to be able to compete and train there is unreal."

title: Heartbreak in New York as Williams sisters turn back the clock, fall just short
text:
Advertisement

SportTennisUS Open Heartbreak in New York as Williams sisters turn back the clock, fall just short Michael Koziol September 5, 2026 — 1:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Some fans have criticised this US Open for the ambient noise emitted by attendees who won’t stop talking during play – particular on its cavernous centre court. But reporters who have been at Arthur Ashe Stadium all week agreed the crowd was much better behaved at Friday night’s blockbuster starring Venus and Serena Williams. They were there to actually watch the game. Serena and Venus Williams turned back the clock in a three-hour doubles thriller at the US Open. Getty Images And so they should be. These are legends of the sport, who turned back the clock and fell agonisingly short in a doubles thriller against Australia’s Maya Joint and Taiwan’s Hao-ching Chan. It was a match that more than lived up to the occasion; getting better over its three hours, and with plenty of quality, exciting rallies that can sometimes go missing in the stop-start, rapid-fire nature of doubles tennis.

Advertisement

On a hot Friday night, New York brought out its stars. Mr Beast, the YouTuber extraordinaire who has amassed more than 500 million subscribers, was on court for the coin toss, while those watching in the stands included Vogue editor and tennis tragic Anna Wintour, Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Andy Dalton and wrestler Mr T. While the crowd may have been respectful during points, it was uproarious between them. From the moment Serena, 44, and Venus, 46, emerged on the court, the parochial New York audience went predictably crazy. The jubilant New York crowd thought the American icons were home and hosed. Getty Images It is here at the US Open that these titans won two of their 14 grand slam doubles trophies; where Venus was a singles champion twice and where Serena picked up six of her 23 singles titles. In short, they are royalty. They last played doubles here in 2022, when they were already in their 40s, losing in the first round. The stands then, as now, were packed to the rafters with fans who thought they may not see the Williams sisters again.

Advertisement

Indeed, Serena retired straight after that US Open, and gave birth to her second daughter, Adira, nearly a year later. This week she told Good Morning America her inspiration to return to the doubles court came from her older daughter, Olympia. “You need to play with Auntie VeVe,” Olympia had urged. “She said it so clear and so calm. She’s like my mom, she doesn’t really talk a lot, but when she does talk, you listen.” Australia’s Maya Joint and Hao-ching Chan of Taiwan high five after a point. AP Photo/Adam Hunger Joint, who is just 20, was born in Michigan to an Australian father, and moved to Melbourne last year. This year, she knocked Serena out of Wimbledon in the first round of the singles draw. Like a classic car that needs a few runs around the block to warm up, the Williams sisters excelled as the match went on, having lost the first set 3-6. Serena got bolder at the net, to her advantage, while Venus improved her ground strokes from the back of the court.

Advertisement

Challenged substantially multiple times on serve in the second, they dug in and, willed on by the home crowd, produced some of the best tennis of the match at the net and from the baseline. Fans roared when, after a truly remarkable rally in the tiebreak, the sisters set up their fourth set point. When they ultimately prevailed to send the match to a decider, the crowd rose instantly to its feet. Serena Williams, 23-time grand slam singles champion and 14-time doubles champ with her sister, on Friday night. AP The third and final set was no less exciting. Down a break early, the Williams sisters clawed their way back to even keel. An expectant crowd rode every wave, gasping as Serena smashed a forehand way long at 4-4, and cheering every winner (and occasionally, a fault from Chan or Joint, which the umpire tried to quell). Related Article US Open ‘Someone is smoking weed’: Sabalenka interrupts US Open match over cannabis smell

Advertisement

People were on their feet as Venus and Serena raced to a 5-0 lead in the deciding tiebreak when victory seemed all but assured. Somehow, they faltered, stymied by costly errors at the final hurdle. The crowd was subdued in defeat, but gave them a standing ovation as they departed. In the end, not much separated the contenders. One too many errant net shots, one or two double faults, a few over-hit forehands. The legends matched their younger counterparts pound for pound, they put on a thrilling show, and the win could have easily been theirs. Speaking on court after the match, Joint praised the “surreal” atmosphere, one she had not experienced before. Playing against such esteemed opponents was “super special”, she said. “I grew up in Michigan, I’ve always looked up to them … I’m lost for words.” Fans left the stadium heartbroken but not disappointed after the Williams sisters were beaten in three sets. Getty Images We often write off older bodies, especially women who have given birth. It is something every elite athlete must grapple with; on the men’s side, Novak Djokovic is doing just that after his first-round exit from the US Open at age 39, having vomited multiple times on court as he appeared to come to grips with his new limitations.

Advertisement

Venus and Serena Williams declined to speak to reporters after the match, so there was no opportunity to parse their thoughts on the gutting loss. But they turned back the clock with style – and though many left the stadium heartbroken, nobody left disappointed. Watch the US Open live on 9GO!, 9NOW and Stan Sport. Kathmandu: Relatives with the grim task of identifying their loved ones missing in Nepal’s catastrophic floods go filing through the gates of Kathmandu’s Maharajgunj Medical Campus, uncertain of what they will see, or what they want to find. The morgue is a stopover for many of the bodies recovered from remote Rasuwa and Nuwakot, the worst hit districts. Forensic teams take DNA samples and attach tags, then send the bodies to temporary mass graves outside the capital, making way for the next batch. Loading For families whose desperate combing of the hospital have come to naught, each load of bodies at the morgue holds closure or promise.

Advertisement

“I hope he is still alive and I don’t find him here,” says 24-year-old Bakhat Pariyar, who is checking for his little brother, Laxman. “But if he is dead, we need to take him home to perform our rituals.” Laxman last made contact with his family at 7.30am on August 26, the day of the flood, near the wiped-out village of Timure. Pariyar says his brother was almost certain to be granted a study visa for the United Kingdom and had wanted to go trekking in the spectacular mountains one last time. Bakhat Pariyar at Kathmandu’s Maharajgunj Medical Campus, moments after looking through pages of photos of unidentified bodies. He is searching for his younger brother Laxman, a student who was last seen in Timure just before flash flooding hit the area. KATE GERAGHTY He is not among the 47 bodies inside. “We will come back when more bodies come in,” Pariyar says. “I don’t know what I will do if I find him.”

Advertisement

The first thing confronting searching relatives is the smell, an utterly overwhelming mix of decomposition and disinfectant. Next, they must pore through A4 sheets of paper, stapled into a booklet, containing the forensic photos of bodies presently being processed. Police in Kathmandu unload bodies of people killed in the flood. KATE GERAGHTY Officials work to identify bodies at the Maharajgunj Medical Campus. KATE GERAGHTY Such photos are also posted on a wall across the road. Most images on both wall and in booklet are of figures so mangled by the flood and bloated from days in the sun and mud that it is difficult to see how any of them may be identified this way.

Advertisement

An official at the morgue says 24 have been identified since last week, though none yet on Friday. Related Article Floods In Nepal, hope gives way to grief. Few are counting on miracles The volume of death is so great for Nepal’s limited resources that bodies lie exposed. We travelled by chance behind a police bus ferrying bodies on Thursday afternoon, and see it again, parked at the morgue, close to 24 hours later with what an official confirms are some of the same bodies (and two rice sacks full of body parts) only now being unloaded. Seven Australian Federal Police identification specialists are due to arrive in Kathmandu at the weekend, adding to a 15-member disaster assistance response team that landed on Friday. A short walk away, people are giving samples of their DNA in the hope they may be able to retrieve family members from the mass graves, and afford them proper Hindu or Buddhist cremation.

The precinct at Tribhuvan University Teaching Hospital also contains the great wall of grief, on which relatives attach posters of their missing. When we visited soon after the disaster, the wall contained a couple of dozen posters. Now, there are hundreds, with more still being added. title: The West’s breathless AI spending spree can end only one way
text:
Advertisement

MoneyInvestingAI Opinion The West’s breathless AI spending spree can end only one way

Jeremy Warner September 5, 2026 — 1:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

But this time is different, right? As every student of investment trends knows, any boom will ultimately culminate in a bust. Yet almost invariably this truism – repeatedly proven by historical experience – is forgotten in the excitement of the boom du jour; or, rather, investors come to believe that in their particular case, the boom is perfectly sustainable. I do know a bubble when I see one, and the current breathless pace of investment in AI is undoubtedly that. iStock Equally invariably, belief in “this time is different” turns out to be flawed. As indeed it will be with the latest technological revolution to engulf the world of commerce: artificial intelligence. I have to confess to being somewhat bewildered by the pace, scale and complexity of the change that AI is bringing about, and readily admit to lacking the expertise to fully understand both the technology and its path to monetisation. I should add that this is not for want of trying.

Advertisement

But I do know a bubble when I see one, and the current breathless pace of investment in AI is undoubtedly that. It’s happening far too fast for the capital markets and the public to accommodate without mishap. Related Article Opinion

Middle East at war Trump is clutching at straws and the world knows it Ah, yes, but actually, say its cheerleaders, it is not nearly as big as some of those seen in the past; and unlike the dotcom boom of the late 1990s, or the British railway mania of the 1840s, it is substantially funded by the existing cash flows of the major tech giants. Both these observations are supported by the facts. At its peak, annual capital spending on railways reached an astonishing 20 per cent of British GDP, and even the investment boom in broadband supporting infrastructure during the 1990s reached close to 2 per cent of US GDP. Current data centre and associated hardware spending is “only” about 1.5 per cent of US GDP, and this is largely being met from the already burgeoning profits of “big tech”. All the same, the suspicion that what we are witnessing is another giant misallocation of capital refuses to go away.

Advertisement

Extreme levels of share price volatility among leading AI operatives already point to a basic, underlying lack of confidence in the highfalutin claims made for the earnings potential of this massive increase in capital spending. Up like a rocket in initial trading after its IPO a couple of months ago, then down like a spent stick, shares in Elon Musk’s SpaceX now trade 17 per cent below the peak they reached shortly after the issue price. News that the company plans to double down on investment in computing power went down badly with investors. They thought they were investing in a rocket company, not another data centre behemoth. Elon Musk at the SpaceX debut. Bloomberg Lately, even the so-called “picks and shovels” trade – the notion that the real money in any gold rush is to be made not by the prospectors themselves but by those selling them the enabling hardware, in this case high-end processing and memory chips – has come off the boil in anticipation of an eventual pronounced slowdown in demand.

Advertisement

So far, there is still no sign of this in announced spending plans, but it doesn’t entirely quell fears of a sudden stop when investors and credit markets abruptly turn off the taps. A number of recent developments have added to these concerns. First and perhaps most important is the advent of our old friend, growing Chinese competition. This first became apparent with the launch in January last year of the Hangzhou-based DeepSeek, said to have been developed at a fraction of the cost of US frontier models but with equally powerful capabilities. Since then, there has been a steady stream of cheap and cheerful launches from China’s AI sector, including Alibaba’s Qwen 3.8 Max, which is said to be better in some respects than Anthropic’s flagship Fable 5. Before that, we’d seen the launch of Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3, again said to be as good as many pricier Western models. Already, these Chinese upstarts are beginning to make significant inroads into Western markets, where their open-source approach to AI is thought perfectly adequate and in some ways better for most needs. Sound familiar? Yes, it follows exactly the same pattern as virtually every industry you care to think of. So much for “first-mover advantage”. In this case, as in many others, it is those slipstreaming in the wake of the pioneers that may reap the bigger harvest.

Advertisement

Not that this has in any way lessened the appetite among US hyperscalers for AI infrastructure investment. The US already has 5400 operational data centres, with many more planned. China, by contrast, has fewer than 500, though they tend to be bigger in scale. Related Article Mergers & acquisitions French trio minted as billionaires as the world’s most valuable company swoops In other words, China seems to be managing the AI transition on much smaller capital outlays than the US and Europe, thereby limiting the squeeze in overall capital spending that the AI leviathan inflicts on other industries and the fallout that might ensue from any slowdown in AI deployment. In the West, there is a real danger of AI becoming a kind of all-consuming black hole that sucks the life out of all other forms of investment. The other factor that should concern investors and lenders is the increasingly vocal public backlash against AI, manifested in sometimes violent local opposition to the construction of more data centres.

Advertisement

This is something quite new to America, which generally has a more positive attitude to cutting-edge industrial development than most other Western economies, and it seems to be directly linked not just to the appalling aesthetics and energy-guzzling characteristics of data centres but to a genuine loathing of the power of the tech giants and what they represent. Small-town America is not taking kindly to the tech bros of Silicon Valley remaking the world in their own image. Even Donald Trump, spooked by the growing number of cybersecurity incidents associated with OpenAI and Anthropic models, has begun to take note, though he qualifies support for more public control with the greater priority of winning the AI arms race with China. “We don’t want to restrict them where all of a sudden we come in second to China,” the US president said last week. “Whoever wins with AI is going to win. That’s how big it is ... I don’t want to restrict them from doing great work.” So the “great work” continues, turbocharged by China snapping at Silicon Valley’s heels. Those paying attention can only sit back and wonder how long this game of beggar-thy-neighbour can continue before cold reality bites.

Advertisement

It’s only just begun, say uber-bulls, pointing to plans for Google to supply Anthropic with more than $US150 billion ($208 billion) in AI chips. The fact that the Google-Anthropic deal relies on a complex “you scratch my back and I’ll scratch yours” money-go-round – always a bad sign – doesn’t seem to bother them. As long as the music is playing, you’ve got to get up and dance, said the chairman of Citigroup just ahead of the global financial crisis. Quite so. A plan to install a life-saving medicine dispenser near Melbourne’s safe injecting room has been scrapped after the local mayor claimed it would encourage drug use on the street rather than inside the medically supervised centre. The Victorian government is investigating locations for a free naloxone dispensing machine in the City of Yarra, as part of a statewide trial to make the vital medication – which can temporarily reverse an opioid overdose – more accessible. A free naloxone dispensing machine that’s been installed at the Alfred Hospital Emergency and Trauma Centre in Melbourne. Ruby Alexander Yarra Mayor Stephen Jolly wrote a letter to Health Minister Ingrid Stitt in June, asking her not to install a dispenser at a proposed site on Victoria Street near the North Richmond medically supervised injecting room. Yarra staff told councillors that Jolly’s letter and a subsequent meeting between the council and the Department of Health is ultimately why the location on Victoria Street is no longer being considered.

The mayor told The Age that while he would support a naloxone machine on-site at the safe injecting room or at the nearby St Vincent’s Hospital, he did not want it along such a major thoroughfare. “If we put [a machine] on Victoria Street … we’re encouraging people to use drugs on Victoria Street rather than go 100 metres to the south to the supervised injecting facility,” Jolly said. “When you whack [a machine] on Victoria Street, where all the locals are and all the traders are … it’s almost like rubbing their nose in it.” In June, the Victorian government announced a statewide trial program of the free 24/7 naloxone machines. Twenty dispensers will be rolled out as part of a wider $95 million program – 10 in Melbourne and 10 in regional Victoria. They will remain in place until June 2027.

Half of the machines have already been installed as part of the trial. A further seven local government areas have been earmarked as locations for the second tranche, but exact locations are yet to be announced. There are still plans to install a machine somewhere in Yarra. A government spokesperson did not answer questions about the specific location, when it would be installed, or whether the letter from Jolly had impacted any decisions. They said that discussions with the council to identify a suitable site commenced in August 2025. Chris Fagan still recalls the days when the Brisbane Lions struggled to attract Gabba crowds. The ground had become a sobering reminder of just how far the club needed to lift themselves out of the gutter. Oh, how times have changed. When the Lions now grace their home turf, there is barely an empty seat. Fans across the state, so typically dominated by rugby league, have galvanised behind the success Fagan has ushered into the city. “I don’t think we should take all the credit for that; I think people at AFL Queensland work pretty hard as well to promote the game and to help all the clubs at local level become stronger. [But] I think the Lions have probably captured the imagination of the football public,” Fagan said. Harris Andrews, Logan Morris, Kai Lohmann with coach Chris Fagan. AFL Photos via Getty Images “I remember early days when we all started on this project together, we might get 15,000 to a game at the Gabba, and there were a lot of empty seats. Now it’s full. I’m really proud that our club’s been able to do that.

Advertisement

“There’s no doubt footy in the state of Queensland is in a much stronger position than it was 10 years ago, and we’ve played a bit of a role in that.” Consecutive premierships from three-straight grand final appearances have come on the back of what is now eight-consecutive September campaigns – a far cry from their cellar-dwelling years in which they reached this stage of the season just once from 2005 to their 2019 finals return. However, assembling the squad and implementing a program to make this decade of triumphs a reality took careful planning. It involved harnessing homegrown talent and forging a succession plan that ensured that if one man succumbed to injury or departed the Den, the next brigade was ready to pick up the slack. True, they have been well-supported by the academy processes, which allow clubs to match Draft bids for their services. However, just 10 of the 44-man squad have come through those pathways, with nine of the 16 Queensland-raised players born within the Lions’ 14 years in the doldrums.

Advertisement

In contrast, seven members of the Lions’ 2003 premiership team grew up in the state, with four born outside Queensland. Related Article AFL Briefing

AFL 2026 AFL and NFL set for high-stakes MCG turf war “We were always just looking for the best players wherever we could find them around the country, but obviously, given we’re a Queensland-based team, the more guys we could get from the state the better,” Fagan said. “We’ve got our people who run our academy who have done a tremendous job in identifying talent and developing talent. It’s important for the team to represent and have within it a lot of Queensland born and bred players.” Intertwined with the vision of a local talent factory taking the AFL by storm were some shrewd recruitment moves to inject more experience into the youthful group.

Advertisement

The addition of Hawthorn champion Luke Hodge from 2018 to 2019 began that shift, with Lachie Neale, Josh Dunkley and Charlie Cameron following suit. In 2026, the new faces have continued to add layers to Brisbane’s charge towards a third-straight premiership, with Sam Draper providing an enigmatic presence at the ruck, while former West Coast captain Oscar Allen has enabled Fagan to deploy three talls in his forward line. Loading Fagan was emphatic that their recruitment strategy should involve identifying “great characters” who would add value to the club’s culture, while labelling those who have joined the outfit as “real difference makers”. But the efficacy of Brisbane’s succession plan may not be realised until 2027, when Neale is expected to line up in Collingwood colours.

The two-time Brownlow Medal winner has endured a tumultuous year off the field following his scandalous marriage breakdown, which ultimately led him to stand down from the co-captaincy. Related Article Exclusive

A-League Women Meet the youngest coach in Australian history on a quest to be ‘best ever’ On the field, however, he has remained one of the game’s leading midfielders – averaging 30 disposals, seven clearances, and more than four inside 50s per game, at a time when fellow star Zac Bailey is weighing up a lucrative move to South Australia. While Fagan stressed that Neale had not confirmed to him that he would be a Magpie next year, he stressed the uncertainty surrounding the All-Australian pairing had not prevented them from galvanising their younger peers. “Obviously, we want to keep them as players, we’re desperate to do that, but it doesn’t change what we do on a daily basis,” he said.

“He [Neale] has had a lot going on, and a lot of it’s really uncomfortable and difficult stuff to deal with … but he’s dealt with it incredibly well. He seems to be one of those people who can compartmentalise his professional life and what’s going on outside it.” Fagan confirmed co-captain Hugh McCluggage would return from a calf issue in the qualifying final clash with the Sydney Swans. Premier David Crisafulli has pitched Queensland’s critical minerals directly to US Vice President JD Vance on his trade mission to Washington DC, declaring it is Queensland’s time to get projects funded. Several other states have received funding injections after US President Donald Trump and the Albanese government signed a multibillion-dollar deal designed to break China’s dominance of the sector. The premier and leaders from five companies this week met with finance agencies and government departments to pitch for funding or commodity purchase agreements. Queensland Premier David Crisafulli meets with US Vice President JD Vance during a trip to the US. David Crisafulli Crisafulli secured a one-on-one meeting with Vance, during which he pitched Queensland’s minerals industry.

Advertisement

“The United States is hungry for critical minerals, and Queensland is open for business. We’ve got momentum and we’ve got projects ready to go. This is our time,” he said in a statement on Saturday. “Queensland is uniquely positioned to deliver, and deliver quickly, with a safe and secure supply chain that our allies can rely on. “Every piece of the puzzle is building to this being Queensland’s time. It doesn’t matter whether it’s developing new industries, encouraging people to relocate offices from other parts of the country to our state, or hosting big events, more people are hearing about Queensland for the first time. We should be proud of that and use it to drive jobs and opportunities for the years ahead.” The Queensland government signed a five-year memorandum of cooperation with California’s government this week. Crisafulli said the partnership would create opportunities for Queensland’s agriculture sector to share knowledge, technology and expertise with California.

Related Article Foreign relations ‘Force posture’: Marles, Hegseth back expanded US military presence in Australia “This is about bringing the best ideas and applying them to a Queensland context, and putting our producers in the box seat to lead the next phases of innovation,” he said. “This agreement creates a pathway for greater cooperation in areas including AgTech, biotechnology, research and productivity, as well as for workers and researchers themselves. “We know innovation is critical to the future of Queensland agriculture, particularly as our producers respond to changing conditions, workforce challenges, and the need to keep improving productivity. “We have an ambitious goal of growing our primary industries to $30 billion by 2030, and this agreement will help us get there.”

Related Article Rare earths Trump’s critical minerals deal unearths a bonanza for Aussie miners Under the Trump-Albanese agreement, the US and Australia will each contribute at least US$1 billion ($1.5 billion) over the next six months to help fund a proposed multibillion-dollar pipeline of investment in Australia and the US. In state parliament last week, Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie said the trade trip was about “being at the forefront” of the conversation with the Trump administration. “We want the critical minerals to come out of Queensland, not Western Australia, not the Northern Territory,” he said. “We want them to come out of Queensland. We want to generate Queensland jobs.” Last month, the ambassador of Finland was eager to offer the Nordic nation’s services to help kick-start Queensland’s minerals production industry. Arto Haapea told this masthead his country – highly regarded for developing mining and production technology – could help facilitate local refining and manufacturing.

Experts have long warned of the lack of economic benefits to a “dig and ship” approach, with the real value coming from onshore processing and refining. The Crisafulli government’s 2026-30 critical minerals strategy flags investment in processing through local refining and manufacturing. No US funding injections have yet been announced for Queensland, however other states have benefited from the partnership. The Pentagon will invest $US400 million ($560 million) in a “world-first” mining project in central-western NSW that produces scandium, a rare critical mineral used in fighter jets, spacecraft and other tools of war. Funding of $200 million in concessional finance for the Alcoa-Sojitz Gallium Recovery Project in Wagerup, Western Australia, and $100 million for the Arafura Nolans project in the Northern Territory was announced in October. title: New Bluey coin will hit you for six
text:
It is an episode celebrated for encapsulating just why Aussies love cricket.

And the highly-acclaimed Bluey episode is being immortalised as the latest addition to the sought-after coin collection.

The Royal Australian Mint has announced it is launching yet another Bluey $1 coin – or dollarbucks as the loveable Heeler family call them.

And it will be based around one of the show's most recent episodes, Cricket.

The new Bluey collector coin, which is based on the episode Cricket. Picture: Royal Australian Mint

Centring around supporting character Rusty, the heartwarming episode shows how practice makes perfect as Bluey's dad Bandit and his mates struggle to bowl out the eager kelpie.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

And one of the memorable moments from the episode features on the new $1, with Rusty sending a fierce drive as Bluey cheers him on.

The new coin launches later this month, with demand expected to be so high that the Mint is running a ballot to secure them.

An uncirculated version of the coin will be available to purchase for $25, while a limited edition silver proof coin inside a cricket ball tin will be sold for $112.50.

Special edition versions will be sold in a cricket ball shaped tin. Picture: Royal Australian Mint

It comes after a collection of $2 coins was launched by Australia Post earlier this year.

"To celebrate a classic Aussie tradition, the Royal Australian Mint presents a fun and colourful new coin design based on the beloved Cricket episode of Bluey," A Royal Australian Mint spokesman said.

Advertisement Advertisement
